index.content:
China Ancient–Present
A narrative-research knowledge base on China from antiquity to the present — courts and capitals, dynastic order and its breakdowns, land and revenue, learning and belief, frontiers and foreign contact, republic and party-state — built from sources as contemporaries wrote and read them, with special room for texts in classical and vernacular Chinese and for foreign accounts of their own day.
Total pages: 15 (15 sources)

The Narrative
Fifteen foundation texts now anchor the shelf. The Republican Qingshi guan (清史馆) draft Qingshi gao (清史稿) walks the Qing house from Nurhaci (努尔哈齐) and the Tianming (天命) state to the Xuantong (宣统) close — annals, treatises, tables, and biographies through tusi (土司), fanbu (籓部), and shuguo (属国). Qian Mu’s (钱穆) wartime university outline Guoshi dagang (国史大纲) narrates one continuous body of Chinese history from archaic Huaxia (华夏) through Qin–Han institutions, literati politics, north–south shifts, Qing “tribal” rule, and the early Republic / resistance horizon. Lü Simian’s (吕思勉) Zhongguo tongshi (中国通史) splits the same long run another way: an upper book of eighteen institutional–cultural topics (marriage and clan through religion) and a lower book of political narrative from the origins of the people to China on the revolutionary road. Sun Wen’s (孫文) 1924 Guangzhou lectures Sanmin zhuyi (三民主義) state the revolutionary-nationalist program — nationalism, people’s rights, and people’s livelihood through sixteen lectures (民生 ending at four). His composite Jianguo fanglüe (建国方略) adds the constructive companion: psychological reconstruction (行易知难), the six industrial plans of 实业计划, the parliamentary primer 民权初步, plus 一大宣言, 建国大纲, and the 总理遗嘱. His life in turn is told in the 1946 Kuomintang-series translated biography Sun Yixian zhuanji (孫逸仙傳記, trans. 徐植仁) — ten periods from the 翠亨 village childhood of 1866 through the 1925 death, covering the London kidnapping, the provisional presidency, the campaign against Yuan Shikai, and the alliance with Soviet Russia. An earlier, contemporary view of Sun comes from the Japanese revolutionary sympathizer Miyazaki Tōten (宮崎滔天) in Dagemingjia Sun Yixian (大革命家孙逸仙, trans. 黄中黄 1903), a chaptered account of Sun and the Xingzhonghui, the London legation imprisonment, and the rivalry between Sun’s party and Kang Youwei’s (康有為) monarchist party, drawn from Miyazaki’s memoir 《三十三年之夢》. His successor at the head of the Nationalist movement is heard directly in the Jiang Jieshi riji (蒋介石日记, 1915–1949), a selective compilation of Chiang Kai-shek’s own dated entries — from the anti-Yuan campaigns and the 1936 Xi’an Incident, through the War of Resistance, the Hong Kong surrender dispute and the 1945 Chongqing talks with Mao, the Marshall Mission, and the 1949 collapse and retreat. On the Communist side, the party-edited Mao Zedong xuanji (毛泽东选集, complete in four volumes) collects Mao Zedong’s own writings from 1925 to 1949 — the class and peasant analyses and the Jiangxi-Soviet strategy of the revolutionary civil wars, On Protracted War and On New Democracy and the Yan’an rectification of the resistance years, and the civil-war campaign directives, On the People’s Democratic Dictatorship, and the 1949 polemics against the US White Paper. Moving into the party-state era, Huang Zheng & Huang Hai’s (黄峥、黄海) 1983 PLA study companion Jianguo dagang lilun jichu (建国大纲理论基础——《邓小平文选》学习讲话) re-appropriates the 建国 vocabulary in the early reform register: eleven lectures through the Selected Works of Deng Xiaoping (邓小平文选) — from re-establishing seeking-truth-from-facts and the shift to economic construction, through the Four Modernizations, Party building, the united front, and the army, to safeguarding Mao’s standing and developing Mao Zedong Thought. The full post-1949 arc is carried by He Qin’s (何沁) Zhonghua Renmin Gongheguo shi (中华人民共和国史, 2nd ed. 1999), an official Higher Education Press textbook spanning the PRC from its 1949 founding — the CPPCC and Common Program, democratic reform and economic recovery, the socialist transformation and Great Leap, the Cultural Revolution, and the reform era through the 14th and 15th Party Congresses and Hong Kong’s 1997 return — to the eve of the 50th anniversary. The architect of the reform era is given his life in Deng Xiaoping shilu (邓小平实录, ed. 李新芝, 1904–1997), a four-volume biographical record — from the French work-study youth and the Long March, through the Taihang and Central Plains campaigns, the Cultural Revolution ordeal, the return to power and the Third Plenum, to his role as chief architect (总设计师) of reform and opening and the 1992 southern tour. The official history is carried to the present by the 2022 Zhonghua Renmin Gongheguo shi (中华人民共和国史, 马工程 key textbook), spanning the PRC from its 1949 founding through the reform era to the COVID-19 pandemic, the poverty-alleviation victory, and the 2021 CPC centenary — the Xi-era authoritative narrative into the 2020s. The economic present is read through Lan Xiaohuan’s (兰小欢) Zhishen shi nei (置身事内, 2021), a Fudan economist’s account of how the Chinese government and economy interact — local government power and investment promotion, the 1994 tax-sharing reform and land finance, the urban-investment platforms and local debt, industrial policy, urbanization and inequality, and the Sino-US trade conflict. Bridging the revolutionary war years in the central party-history office’s own voice is Zhongguo Gongchandang lishi (中国共产党历史) 第一卷下册 (Central Party History Research Office, 2011): from the full outbreak of the War of Resistance in July 1937 through base-area consolidation, the postwar contest of two destinies, the Liberation War’s strategic turn and decisive campaigns, to the Seventh Central Committee’s Second Plenum at Xibaipo and the September 1949 threshold of the new state. sources/chiang-kai-shek-diary-1915-1949.content:
Chiang Kai-shek’s Diary: Selected Entries 1915–1949 (Jiang Jieshi riji 蒋介石日记) — Chiang Kai-shek 蒋介石, compiled by 偶然童子
What this is
蒋介石日记（1915-1949） (Jiang Jieshi riji, “Chiang Kai-shek’s Diary 1915–1949”) is a curated compilation of dated diary entries attributed to Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石 / 蒋中正; here addressed throughout as 余, “I”). The text is framed as authored by 蒋介石 and compiled / prepared by ☆偶然童子☆ — an unofficial internet compiler’s e-text, not an archival edition. It selects 185 dated entries spread across nineteen years of a thirty-four-year span, pairing each date with Chiang’s recorded reflections on the events around it.
This is not the full, continuous diary. The genuine Chiang diary manuscripts are preserved at the Hoover Institution (Stanford) and were long kept sealed; this file is a selective popular compilation that jumps between years and annotates the text. It should be read as a widely circulated selection of diary passages, not a complete scholarly transcript. Its value for this wiki is that it preserves, in Chiang’s own first-person voice, his wartime and civil-war framing of events — the Japanese invasion and surrender, the Chinese Communist Party (共匪 / 共党 in his usage), the Marshall Mission, and the 1949 collapse.

How it is organized
The text proceeds chronologically by year, with several years subdivided (e.g. 1916年 1 / 1916年 2; 1937年 1–8; 1938年 1–4; 1942年 1–2; 1943年 3; 1945年 5–8; 1946年 4; 1949年 2). Under each year run dated entries in 【月 日】 brackets. Two entries are extended set-pieces: the 西安半月记 fragment (December 12, 1936, the Xi’an Incident) and the 1938 元旦 essay on the war.
Chapter breakdown (year by year)
Style: English title + (pinyin + 中文) + multi-line gloss of what Chiang’s selected entries record. All views are Chiang’s own first-person framing, as preserved by the compiler.
Early revolutionary years (1915–1919)
1915 年. Brief, event-anchored notes: Yuan Shikai accepting Japan’s Twenty-One Demands (5月9日); 杨度、孙毓筠、严复 et al. launching the 筹安会 to promote monarchy (8月14日); the party (总理 = Sun Yat-sen) dispatching fundraisers abroad for the anti-Yuan campaign (9月30日); Cai E (蔡锷) organizing the 护国军 uprising in Yunnan (12月25日).
1916 年 1–2. Chiang’s service in the anti-Yuan revolutionary northeast army. The assassination of Chen Qimei (陳其美) by Yuan’s agents in a Japanese resident’s home (5月18日) — “余哭之哀，收其尸以归…自撰文祭之.” Then long operational passages from his time with the 中华革命党东北军 headquarters at 潍县 (Weixian): daily orders, inspection tours, telegraph traffic, handling discipline complaints against his troops, coordinating with Japanese guard detachments — vivid records of an officer’s routine in the anti-Yuan campaign.
1917–1919 年. Scattered entries: the early revolutionary period and events around the party’s rebuilding. (Compiled entries thin for these years.)
The Central Plains War and prewar crisis (1930–1936)
1930 年. Reflections amid the Central Plains War (中原大战): the flux of alliances among warlords (“联此制彼或联彼制此，皆非正本之道”), the need to strengthen one’s own forces and let rivals exhaust each other, and wartime resolve (“唯有坚忍镇静，维系军心…若至万不得已，唯有一死以报党国”). Later entries note 东北 forces joining the central front in effect if not in open combat.
1931–1935 年. Sparse selection: the Mukden Incident era (1931 九一八) and the subsequent years of Japanese pressure and internal consolidation. (Compiled entries are light.)
1936 年. The run-up to the Xi’an Incident. Chiang despairs over the national humiliation and counsels forbearance toward Japan (“三年之内，倭寇不能灭中国…但此时当不可不隐忍”), and increasingly distrusts Zhang Xueliang (汉卿 / 张学良) over his reluctance to campaign against the communists. The centerpiece is the 西安半月记 fragment (12月12日): Chiang’s own account of the night of the mutiny — gunfire at the Huaging Pool residence, his escape over the wall and up the mountain, and the dawning realization of a planned coup rather than a local mutiny. Followed by relief that the central authorities were managing the crisis (12月16日).
The War of Resistance (1937–1938)
1937 年 (8 month-sections). From the Marco Polo Bridge (七七, 7月8日 entry) through the fall campaigns. The entries chart Chiang’s decision to resist, the shift of the war to Shanghai and the interior, and his conviction that the conflict must be long and that China’s perseverance would ultimately turn the international situation.
1938 年 (4 month-sections). Chiang’s wartime diary at length:

元旦 essay on foreign policy: neither Japan (倭祸急) nor the Soviet danger (俄患隐) should be relied upon; China must stand self-sufficient and independent.
Refusal to capitulate — “与其屈服而亡，不如战败而亡” — and dismissal of Japanese threats to deny recognition to the National Government.
The propaganda value of the Taierzhuang victory (台儿庄胜利, 4月30日) for morale.
Dismay at internal wavering (e.g. 高宗武’s freelancing) and at the maneuvers among 近卫, 坂垣, 宇垣 over whether to seek a negotiated settlement with China.
Faith that Japan’s failure to win quickly was fatal, and that a second world war loomed in which China must prepare its role.

Wartime diplomacy and the end of the war (1940–1945)
1940 年 5. Note of US $100 million loan to China (12月7日), half in currency-stabilization support — Chiang credits Roosevelt’s genuine assistance and marks it as the most substantial international help since the war began.
1942–1943 年. The war in the Pacific context. (Compiled entries selective.)
1945 年 5–8. The end of the war:

Hong Kong surrender dispute (8月26–28日, 8月31日, 9月1日): Chiang insists, as China Theater supreme commander, on appointing a British officer to receive the Japanese surrender in Hong Kong; he resists Britain’s refusal, and records satisfaction that Britain finally accepted the appointment.
The Chongqing talks with Mao Zedong (毛泽东 / 共毛): Chiang’s policy of sincere treatment toward Mao (8月28日), his insistence on the unity of government and military command as the non-negotiable center (8月29日), and his running record of the negotiations — frustration over Communist troop-strength demands (the 48 vs 28 divisions dispute, 9月12日, 9月17日), distrust of Communist intentions in the occupied territories (9月24日), and the farewell meetings with Mao before his return to Yan’an (10月9–11日).
The surrender ceremony at Nanjing on the anniversary of the Guangzhou Uprising (9月9日), set against Chiang’s worries about Soviet occupation of Manchuria, unrest in Xinjiang, and the unresolved Outer Mongolia question.
The atomic bomb and Soviet entry into the war (8月31日): Chiang praises science’s power to end the world’s wars, but condemns Soviet opportunism in declaring war on Japan.

The Marshall Mission and the civil war (1946)
1946 年 4. The collapse of the Marshall Mission mediation. Chiang records that Marshall, disturbed by the CPC’s “July 7 declaration,” still leaned toward accommodating the communists while pressuring the Nationalists (7月13日). (Compiled entries selective for this year.)
The collapse and 1949 (1949 年 2, tail)
The compilation closes in 1949 with the Nationalist collapse and Chiang’s retirement/retreat:

Entries on the Communist rejection of the Li Zongren government and the failure of the peace talks (2月5日, 3月28日, 4月17日, 4月30日): Chiang scorns the “surrenderist” faction and the peace negotiators, and interprets the breakdown of talks as the moment the Republic’s vitality and the renewal of the national revolution must be sought.
The China White Paper (8月10日): Chiang denounces Marshall and Acheson for seeking to cover their China-policy failure by destroying US–China friendship, calling the 1949 White Paper a stain on American history.
Li Zongren’s flight (11月21日): Chiang condemns Li’s refusal to resign or return, judging his conduct selfish and contemptible.
Year-end resolution (12月25日): “从前种种，譬如昨日死，今日种种，犹如今日生” — the party, politics, economy, military, diplomacy, and education have all failed; he resolves to transform the party, reorganize the army, and begin anew.

The text ends with 【完】.
Relation to the other sources
This is the first diary / personal-account source on the shelf, and the first centered on the Nationalist (KMT) leader himself rather than on Sun Yat-sen’s doctrine or the Qing/PRC institutional histories:

























SourceAngle三民主義, 建国方略Sun Yat-sen’s program (1924)孫逸仙傳記Sun’s life as told in a translated biography蒋介石日记 (this file)The post-Sun KMT leader’s own wartime and civil-war reflections (1915–1949)建国大纲理论基础 (1983)PRC-era re-appropriation of the 建国 vocabulary under Deng
Read together, the Sun sources give the republican program and the party’s founding story; this diary shows the second-generation KMT leader who inherited that program and led China through the war with Japan and into the civil war and retreat to Taiwan.
Source notes

Provenance caution: This is a popular compiled e-text (☆偶然童子☆ 整理制作), not the authoritative Hoover Institution edition of the Chiang diaries. It is selective, lightly annotated by the compiler, and partially censored (sensitive characters rendered 胤). Treat dates and phrasing as transcribed from the circulated compilation; for scholarly citation the Hoover manuscripts are the reference.
Language: Chinese (traditional/simplified mixed), with editorial glosses; native PDF text layer is clean.
Not done at ingest: entity / event / concept pages (await Proceed).
Category: republican-era / wartime personal account — complements the Sun texts and the general histories.

sources/dagemingjia-sun-yixian-miyazaki.content:
The Great Revolutionary Sun Yat-sen (Dagemingjia Sun Yixian 大革命家孙逸仙) — Miyazaki Tōten 宮崎滔天, trans. Huang Zhonghuang 黄中黄
What this is
大革命家孙逸仙 (Dagemingjia Sun Yixian, “The Great Revolutionary Sun Yat-sen”) is a Chinese edition of the celebrated Japanese revolutionary sympathizer Miyazaki Tōten’s (宮崎滔天, also 白浪庵滔天) account of Sun Yat-sen, translated by 黄中黄 (Huang Zhonghuang). It belongs to the body of early twentieth-century literature in which Japanese and Chinese activists exchanged accounts of the Chinese revolutionary movement. The work derives from Miyazaki’s memoir 《三十三年之夢》 (“Thirty-three Years’ Dream”) and presents Sun as the founder-leader of the revolutionary party, set against the broader theme of whether China could be reborn through revolution.
The present file is a republication of the translation — a “第A05版 (新闻·真相)” / 都市女报 newspaper-style scan of a DuXiu-sourced document (77 image pages). It opens with a series of prefaces (黄中黄自序, a Chinese sympathizer’s 序, 滔天原序, and 滔天原自序) followed by a chaptered narrative.

How it is organized (this edition)
From the TOC (p. 15):

























ChapterTitleNotes第一章孫逸仙之略歴及其革命Sun’s career and his revolution第二章孫黨與康黨Sun’s party vs. Kang Youwei’s party第三章南洋之風雲The storm in the South Seas (and later sections)
Within 第一章 the TOC lists: 興中會首領 (leader of the Xingzhonghui), 使館之囚 (imprisonment in the [London] legation), 陳白與白浪滔天 (Chen [Shaobai] and Tōten), 支那國民與共和政治 (the Chinese people and republican government), 共和政治須統一英雄之方法 (republican government needs the method of unifying heroes), 支那之興亡與人道之消長 (China’s rise and fall and the waxing and waning of humanity), 品會楊之比較. 第二章 covers 康有為 (Kang Youwei), 革命之急先鋒, 戊戌事變與康黨 (the 1898 Coup and Kang’s party), 康有為之來, 滔天之革命論, 革命與改革之比較, 保皇亦須流血 (monarchism too requires blood), 康孫聯合之夢想 (the dream of uniting Kang and Sun), 康有為與西后, 萬木草堂, 衣帶詔與…電, 小國會, 康絕孫 (Kang breaks with Sun), 日本人之康, 康拒孫, 康有為與李鴻章.
Prefaces
黄中黄自序 (translator’s preface). Written in the voice of the translator, dated 共和 (Minguo-equivalent dating in the OCR reads “共和…千六百十四年…月二十日” — the standard 1903 date of the translation). It argues that Sun Yat-sen is not merely a private person but a newly discovered name of new China — that “without Sun Yat-sen China cannot be reborn,” and that what is named 孫逸仙 is the substance through which China’s renewal is to be achieved. It frames the work as a correction to those who would dismiss Sun and as a statement of the connection between Sun and China’s future.
序 (by a Chinese sympathizer). Recalls that four years earlier Sun seemed to Cantonese merely a “sea pirate of the Guangzhou bay,” then recounts how Miyazaki Tōten, the Japanese “eastern-sea knight,” sought out revolutionary talent in China, encountered Sun, and came to revere him — positioning Sun as one who, before the Qing’s corruption was even exposed (before 甲午/乙未, 1894–95), staked his life on restoring the fatherland, bearing the competition of the race, and proclaiming the rights of man.
滔天原序 (Miyazaki Tōten’s preface, signed 孫文逸仙 拜序). A preface that in Miyazaki’s framing casts him as a latter-day eastern knight (東海俠客) who, like a patron of a new 李世民, travels China to find heroes — here Sun — to build a great undertaking for Asia and for the survival of the Yellow race. It speaks of Miyazaki returning from his journeys to record what he saw, for those concerned with the fate of Asia.
滔天原自序 (Miyazaki Tōten’s own preface). Miyazaki’s personal statement of purpose: he embraces the “world as one family” ideal, holds that true ideals are realizable (not dreams), and declares himself a world revolutionary and a social revolutionary. He argues that land is not man-made but heaven’s gift to all, and therefore should not be monopolized by a few — the theoretical ground he says compelled him to act. He records his resolve to use China as the base of “strength” for realizing his ideals, and the price he paid: the Philippine affair, imprisonment in Singapore, expulsion from the Straits Settlements and from Hong Kong, the abortive revolutionary armies, the 孫逸仙 (Sun Yat-sen) affair, and the internal dissension among comrades — all of which he says he set down in 《三十三年之夢》, for “life is a dream.”
Chapter breakdown
Style: English title + (pinyin + 中文) + multi-line gloss of the chapter’s content as recovered from the OCR body.
第一章 — Sun Yat-sen’s career and his revolution (孫逸仙之略歴及其革命)
Opening on Sun as 興中會首領 (leader of the Xingzhonghui / Revive China Society), the chapter narrates Sun’s early revolutionary career — his organizing, the pre-甲午 context, and the 1896 London legation imprisonment (使館之囚), a set-piece of Sun’s biography. It pairs 陳白 (Chen Shaobai, 陳少白) with 白浪滔天 (Miyazaki) as the associates who aided Sun, then moves to reflective essays: 支那國民與共和政治 argues about the Chinese people and republicanism; 共和政治須統一英雄之方法 reflects on how republican rule must unify “heroes”; 支那之興亡與人道之消長 ties China’s fortunes to the fortunes of humanity; and 品會楊之比較 compares figures (likely Sun / Kang circles or revolutionary organizations) as a set of contrasts.
第二章 — Sun’s party and Kang’s party (孫黨與康黨)
The chapter sets Sun Yat-sen’s revolutionary party (孫黨) against Kang Youwei’s (康有為) reformist/monarchist party (康黨). It opens on 康有為, then 革命之急先鋒 (the vanguard of revolution) and 戊戌事變與康黨 (the 1898 Reform Movement and its coup, and Kang’s party’s fate). 康有為之來 recounts Kang’s arrival abroad; 滔天之革命論 gives Miyazaki’s own theory of revolution; 革命與改革之比較 contrasts revolution and reform; 保皇亦須流血 argues that even monarchism would require bloodshed. 康孫聯合之夢想 treats the once-hoped union of Kang and Sun; 康有為與西后 and 萬木草堂 touch Kang’s relation to the Empress Dowager and his famous academy; 衣帶詔與…電 alludes to the purported secret edict and telegrams; 小國會 a “small parliament.” The chapter closes on the split: 康絕孫 (Kang breaks with Sun), 日本人之康 (the Japanese and Kang), 康拒孫 (Kang rejects Sun), and 康有為與李鴻章 (Kang and Li Hongzhang).
第三章 and onward — The storm in the South Seas (南洋之風雲)
The narrative moves to the overseas Chinese communities of Southeast Asia and the revolutionary fundraising and organizing among them. The OCR body shows episodes of Miyazaki’s and Sun’s activity in Hong Kong, the Straits Settlements, and the South Seas — including confrontations with colonial authorities (the Singapore imprisonment and expulsion, the Hong Kong expulsion mentioned in the prefaces), and the condition of the revolutionary forces. Later pages record the abortive uprising attempts and the difficulties of coordinating secret societies (三合會, 哥老會) with the revolutionary program.
Relation to the other sources
This is the second foreign-authored account of Sun Yat-sen on the shelf, alongside 孫逸仙傳記:





















SourceAuthor / angle三民主義, 建国方略Sun’s own program (1924)孫逸仙傳記 (trans. 徐植仁, 1946)Western biography translated into Chinese大革命家孙逸仙 (this file)Japanese revolutionary sympathizer’s (宮崎滔天) contemporary account, translated 1903
Where 孫逸仙傳記 is a full life told by an outside Western observer, 大革命家孙逸仙 is a contemporary Japanese voice writing in the 1890s–1900s, close to the events and to Sun himself — valuable for the early revolutionary network, Sun–Kang rivalry, and the pan-Asian dimension. Together the two biographies and the two doctrinal texts give the wiki both the doctrine and multiple contemporary framings of Sun.
Source notes

Authorship: The Japanese author is 宮崎滔天 (Miyazaki Tōten, also known as 白浪庵滔天); the Chinese translation is by 黄中黄, with an edition note crediting “（日）白浪庵滔天著；黄中黄译.” The text derives from Miyazaki’s memoir 三十三年之夢 and circulated as a chaptered biography of Sun.
Provenance: This scan is a newspaper-style republication (“第A05版·新闻·真相”, 都市女报) of a DuXiu-sourced document. OCR is vertical traditional Chinese at medium quality.
Language: Chinese (the translation), traditional/vertical in the scan; original Japanese source text not present here.

sources/deng-xiaoping-lushi-li-xinzhi.content:
Deng Xiaoping: A Record of His Life (Deng Xiaoping shilu 邓小平实录), 1904–1997, complete in four volumes — ed. Li Xinzhi 李新芝
What this is
《邓小平实录》(1904—1997) (Deng Xiaoping shilu, “Deng Xiaoping: A Record of His Life”) is a four-volume biography of Deng Xiaoping (邓小平) covering his entire life, 1904–1997, edited by 李新芝 (Li Xinzhi) and published by 北京联合出版公司 (Beijing United Publishing Company). The edition is the 改革开放40周年纪念版 (“40th Anniversary of Reform and Opening” commemorative edition, 2018), issued in four physical volumes.
The work is organized as a period-by-period life record. Each of the ten parts (编) that span the four volumes is divided into recurring subsections: 历程 (course / career — the chronological narrative), 交往 (relations — Deng’s dealings with key figures), and 珍闻 (anecdotes — vignettes from the period). This makes it a biographical chronicle built from career narrative, relationship portraits, and illustrative episodes, in the voice of a PRC biographical compendium.
The four volumes and their year spans:

邓小平实录1：1904—1945 (early life through the War of Resistance)
邓小平实录2：1945—1966 (civil war through the early PRC and the general-secretary years)
邓小平实录3：1966—1982 (the Cultural Revolution decade and the return to power / rectification)
邓小平实录4：1982—1997 (the “chief architect” years and old age)

How it is organized






























VolumePartsSpan邓小平实录1第一编 早年岁月 · 第二编 红军时期 · 第三编 立马太行1904–1945邓小平实录2第四编 逐鹿中原 · 第五编 新中国成立初期 · 第六编 十年总书记1945–1966邓小平实录3第七编 十年危难 · 第八编 拨乱反正1966–1982邓小平实录4第九编 总设计师 · 第十编 晚年情怀1982–1997
Within each 编, the subsections run 历程 (course) → 交往 (relations) → 珍闻 (anecdotes).
Chapter breakdown (by part)
Style: English title + (pinyin + 中文) + multi-line gloss of the period’s content. The names below are the article/entry titles as they appear in the volume table of contents.
第一编 — Early years (早年岁月, 1904–1927)
历程 (course). From his native 古城广安 (Guang’an), his ancestors’ traces, and his parents, through his 少年时光 (youth), 走出夔门 (leaving Sichuan through the Kuimen gorge), the hard life in France (在法国的艰苦生活) during his work-study years, joining the Chinese Communist Youth League in Europe (参加旅欧中国少年共产党), study at Moscow Sun Yat-sen University (在莫斯科中山大学), and service as political department head at the Zhongshan Military School (中山军事学校政治处长).
交往 (relations). Early relationships: with Zhou Enlai (视若兄长—与周恩来), his two mothers, his teacher Wang Yunsong, Li Fuchun and Cai Chang, Feng Yuxiang, and Zhang Xiyuan (his first wife; 人世间的真情—与张锡瑗).
珍闻 (anecdotes). 第一次远洋 (the first ocean voyage), his birthday in distress, his lively temperament, the Paris café, his love of football, and the blue-and-white-striped scarf.
第二编 — The Red Army period (红军时期, 1927–1937)
历程. 进入首脑机关 (entering the central organs), participating in the August 7th Meeting (参加八七会议), serving as Party Central secretary-general (党中央秘书长), becoming a 25-year-old political commissar, the advance into Jingxi (进军靖西), leading the agrarian revolution (主持土地革命), the Pingma military reorganization (指导平马整训), the thousand-mile campaigns (千里转战), entering southern Jiangxi under emergency orders, serving as the first “official” of the Red capital (首任红都”京官”), the “Deng, Mao, Xie, Gu” affair (“邓、毛、谢、古”事件), the “Red Star” newspaper, the Long March (长征途中), and arriving in northern Shaanxi.
交往. With Mao Zedong (毛泽东的功绩是第一位的—与毛泽东), Wang Jiaxiang, Luo Ronghuan, Zhang Yunyi, Li Mingrui, Wei Baqun, and He Jinnian.
珍闻. Leading the singing of the Internationale, curing illness with pumpkin, escorting Comrade Deng, the lamplight of the Kuixing Tower, the friendship of the Youjiang, the battle at Meihua, and eliminating evil-doers.
第三编 — Taking command in Taihang (立马太行, 1937–1945)
历程. 奔赴抗日战场 (rushing to the anti-Japanese battlefield), establishing the mobilization committees, upholding independence and self-reliance (坚持独立自主), leading the resistance and the anti-reactionary struggles, serving in the Hundred Regiments Offensive (在百团大战中), inspecting the Taiyue and Zhongtiao regions, becoming secretary of the Taihang sub-bureau (出任太行分局书记), presiding over the Wencun Conference, and leading base-area construction (领导根据地建设).
交往. The fifty-year comradeship with Liu Bocheng (战友情谊五十年—与刘伯承), and dealings with Peng Dehuai, Xu Xiangqian, and Li Da.
珍闻. Vignettes of the Taihang base-area years.
第四编 — The Central Plains campaigns (逐鹿中原, 1945–1949)
历程. The civil-war campaigns: the struggle for the Central Plains and the advance to the Dabie Mountains with Liu Bocheng, and the run-up to the decisive campaigns that led to the founding of the PRC.
第五编 — The early PRC (新中国成立初期, 1949–1956)
历程. The founding years: the southwest region (Chongqing and the Second Field Army’s governance of the southwest), the establishment of the new state, and the consolidation of the People’s Republic in its early period. (Sections include his role in leading the southwest and the early state’s recovery and transformation.)
第六编 — Ten years as General Secretary (十年总书记, 1956–1966)
历程. Deng’s decade as General Secretary of the CPC Central Committee (1956–1966): the Eighth Party Congress, the Great Leap era, the adjustment years, and his role in party and state leadership before the Cultural Revolution.
第七编 — Ten years of peril (十年危难, 1966–1976)
历程. The Cultural Revolution decade: Deng’s fall, his exile, the period of peril, and his rehabilitation — including the 1973 restoration and his 1975 comprehensive rectification work before the “Criticize Deng, Counterattack the Right-Deviationist Reversal of Verdicts” campaign.
第八编 — Setting things right (拨乱反正, 1976–1982)
历程. After the fall of the Gang of Four (1976): Deng’s full return, the Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee (十一届三中全会) and the shift to reform and opening, the reversal of unjust verdicts, and the restoration of the party line — the decisive turn of the reform era.
第九编 — The chief architect (总设计师, 1982–1989)
历程. Deng as the “chief architect” (总设计师) of reform and opening: the 12th, 13th, and 14th Party Congresses, the establishment of socialism with Chinese characteristics, the special economic zones, and the deepening of the reform program into the late 1980s.
第十编 — Late-life feelings (晚年情怀, 1989–1997)
历程. Deng’s later years (1989–1997): the post-1989 consolidation, the 1992 southern tour (南巡) and its call to speed up reform, the establishment of the socialist market economy, and his final years, closing with his death in 1997.
Relation to the other sources
This is the first full biography of Deng Xiaoping on the shelf, and the direct personal counterpart to the focused Deng-era study text:

Where the PRC history gives the institutional survey and the 1983 study gives Deng’s theory, 邓小平实录 gives the man himself — from the French work-study youth and the Long March, through the Taihang and Central Plains campaigns, the Cultural Revolution ordeal, the return to power, and the reform era he designed. Together these complete the PRC half of the shelf around its central leader.
Source notes

Nature: A PRC biographical compendium (edited, 2018 commemorative edition). It is celebratory in framing (Deng as “总设计师”), not a critical academic biography. Use it as a PRC-era biographical source in the party’s own register.
Language: simplified Chinese digital text; clean (high confidence).

sources/guoshi-dagang-qian-mu.content:
Outline of National History (Guoshi dagang 国史大纲) — Qian Mu (钱穆)
What this book is
Guoshi dagang (国史大纲, Outline of National History) is Qian Mu’s (钱穆, courtesy name Binsi 宾四) single-volume university-level outline of Chinese history written as a gangmu (纲目) textbook: bold gang (纲, main heads) carry the narrative skeleton; indented notes and inline parentheses supply evidence, dates, and asides. The draft digital object here is the two-volume complete set (quan 2 ce 全2册) from the Qian Mu xiansheng quanji (钱穆先生全集 / 钱宾四先生全集) new collated edition (xin jiaoben 新校本) published by Jiuzhou chubanshe (九州出版社, Beijing), ISBN 9787510809941 — a mainland reset of the Taiwan Lianjing (联经) collected-works text.
The book’s origin, as the edition’s chuban shuoming (出版说明, publisher’s note) recounts, is Qian’s Beijing University (Beijing daxue 北京大学) Chinese general history course (Zhongguo tongshi 中国通史) from autumn Republic year 22 (民国二十二年, 1933). After years of rotating specialists, the university asked one lecturer to hold the full survey. Qian taught four years at Beida, then two more at Southwest Associated University (Xinan lianda 西南联大) after the Lugouqiao (芦沟桥, Marco Polo Bridge) crisis of 1937 drove the northern schools south. Colleague Chen Mengjia (陈梦家) urged a textbook for the wartime generation. From May 1938 to June 1939 Qian wrote in seclusion at a villa by Yanquan xiasi (岩泉下寺) outside Yiliang (宜良), Yunnan, using thick notebooks of primary excerpts he had accumulated since Beida. The manuscript — eight bian (编, parts), forty-six zhang (章, chapters), roughly half a million characters — went to Shangwu yinshuguan (商务印书馆, Commercial Press). Lü Simian (吕思勉), Qian’s former middle-school teacher, did a final Shanghai proof; he praised especially the northern–southern economic transfer chapters and the long arc from Wei–Jin tuntian (魏晋屯田, military-agricultural colonies) through Tang zuyongdiao (租庸调). Censorship delayed first issue until June 1940 (Republic 29): reviewers wanted “Hong-Yang zhi luan” (洪杨之乱) rewritten as “Taiping tianguo” (太平天国); Qian refused wholesale renaming and kept the draft wording. Early copies reached Free China via Haiphong; later a Chongqing “national-crisis” (guonan 国难) edition circulated.
This is not a multi-juan dynastic zhengshi (正史). It is a synthetic national outline from deep antiquity through the Anti-Japanese War and the opening of the Republic, written so a student can see one continuous body (yi da ti 一大体) — institutions, economy, thought, and “international” pressure — without drowning in person-by-person annals.
How the book asks to be read
Before the long yinlun (引论, introduction) stand four “beliefs” the reader is asked to hold: a citizen should know the country’s past; knowledge should carry wenqing yu jingyi (温情与敬意, warmth and respect); one should reject blank nihilism toward that past and the pose of standing at history’s absolute summit; national “improvement” without those habits is likened to the reform of a conquered or semi-colonial people. The yinlun itself (~20,000 characters) states method: hunt the locus of change in each age (Warring States → thought; Qin–Han → political institutions; Wei–Jin → social economy), because “where change is, there is historical spirit.” Form is deliberately spare textbook gangmu, not exhaustive chronicle.
Front matter in this EPUB also includes the Jiuzhou xin jiaoben note, the long chuban shuoming on composition and print history, and editorial matter on maps by Wang Hui (王恢) and the advice to pair the outline with Qian’s Zhongguo wenhua shi daolun (中国文化史导论, Introduction to the cultural history of China). Beida’s old Zhongguo tongshi cankao cailiao (中国通史参考材料) of primary extracts is not reprinted in the collected works by Qian’s wish.
Raw text
wiki/raw/guoshi-dagang-qian-mu.txt — about 425,000 characters, 8,500 lines, stripped from the EPUB XHTML (nulls removed). NCX supplies the full gangmu tree (8 bian / 46 zhang plus section heads). EPUB copy kept under sources/.

Part I — Archaic culture; the Three Dynasties
Di yi bian 第一编　上古文化三代之部
Chapter 1 — Cradle of Zhongyuan Huaxia culture; beginnings of Chinese history; Yu–Xia
Zhongyuan Huaxia wenhua zhi faxiang; Zhongguo shi zhi kaishi; Yu Xia shidai（中原華夏文化之發祥；中國史之開始；虞夏時代）
Opens the national story in the Central Plains (Zhongyuan 中原) under the label Huaxia (華夏). Sections move from modern exploration of high antiquity (Paleolithic / Neolithic / Yinxu 殷墟 finds as the book frames them) to the geographic “birth” of that culture, then Xia (夏) king-lists and calendrical estimates, then major Xia events. The tone is outline-critical: what can be said from tradition and from early twentieth-century archaeology, not a romance of sage-kings alone.
Chapter 2 — A new dynasty on the lower Yellow River: Shang–Yin
Huanghe xiayou zhi xin wangchao; Yin Shang shidai（黃河下游之新王朝；殷商時代）
Shang / Yin (商 / 殷) royal genealogy and chronology; conjectures on settlement geography; cultural inferences (bronze-age elite world as the outline needs it); Yin–Zhou (殷周) relations as the hinge to the next order.
Chapter 3 — Rise of the feudal empire: Western Zhou
Fengjian diguo zhi chuangxing; Xizhou xingwang（封建帝國之創興；西周興亡）
Western Zhou (周) king-list; early fengjian (封建, enfeoffment) — including classic eastern placements such as Lu (鲁) and Qi (齐) that push Zhou power toward the sea, and Jin (晋) on the old Xia ruins as a north–south corridor; continued eastward expansion; killing of Youwang (幽王) and Pingwang’s (平王) move east (dongqian 东迁) that opens the Spring and Autumn world.

Part II — Spring and Autumn and Warring States
Di er bian 第二编　春秋战国之部
Chapter 4 — The age of ba politics: Spring and Autumn
Bazheng shiqi; Chunqiu shimo（霸政時期；春秋始末）
Periodization of Chunqiu (春秋): pre-hegemon decades; the long ba (霸, hegemon) run from Qi Huan (齐桓) and Jin Wen (晋文); later decline into dafu zhizheng (大夫执政, ministerial rule); a closing sketch of general cultural conditions. Classic themes such as rangyi (攘夷, resisting “barbarian” pressure) appear as structural headings inside the outline.
Chapter 5 — A new landscape of military-state struggle: Warring States
Junguo douzheng zhi xin jumian; Zhanguo shimo（軍國鬥爭之新局面；戰國始末）
Zhanguo (战国) chronology and stages; the shift from zongfa fengjian (宗法封建, kin-based enfeoffment) to the xin junguo (新军国, new military state) — manpower, law, territory, and diplomacy as one package of change.
Chapter 6 — Rise of free learning among the people: pre-Qin masters
Minjian ziyou xueshu zhi xingqi; Xian Qin zhuzi（民間自由學術之興起；先秦諸子）
For Qian, the deepest Zhanguo change is private, non-temple scholarship. Spring and Autumn learning is still guizu xue (贵族学, aristocratic learning) rooted in zongfa (宗法), ancestral temples, and the shi (史) / temple invocator as the old “only scholar.” Then Ru (儒, classicists) and Mo (墨) rise; academic orientations turn; “shi spirit” runs high; nobles keep guests (yangxian 养贤); among commoner thinkers the outline sorts types (ascetic Mo-line, non-office “slick” scholars, legal-technocratic office-seekers / zongheng 纵横, righteous Ru office, etc.). This chapter is the book’s charter for treating thought as historical structure, not ornament.

Part III — Qin and Han
Di san bian 第三编　秦汉之部
Chapter 7 — Creating the unified government: Qin rise and fall; Han beginnings
Dayitong zhengfu zhi chuangjian; Qin dai xingwang yu Hanshi chuqi（大一統政府之創建；秦代興亡與漢室初起）
Qin–Han king-lists; “coagulation” of state and people; first appearance of a unified government and its collapse; emergence of a pingmin zhengfu (平民政府, commoner-staffed regime) under early Han. Institutional creation is stressed: dismantling fengjian, establishing junxian (郡县, commandery–county), melting aristocratic vs commoner estates as pure legal casts.
Chapter 8 — Civil evolution of the unified government: from Han Wudi to Wang Mang
Tongyi zhengfu wenzhi zhi yanjin; you Han Wudi zhi Wang Mang（統一政府文治之演進；由漢武帝至王莽）
Social baseline of early Western Han (farmers and nubi 奴婢 still near older burdens: shui 税 / rent, yi 役 / labour, fu 赋 / military levies). Early government and scholars; beginnings of a civil ideal at the centre; Han Wu (汉武) “fugu genghua” (复古更化, restore antiquity / renew transformation); a shiren zhengfu (士人政府, literati government) from Zhao–Xuan–Yuan–Cheng; Han Ru political thought; Wang Mang (王莽) receiving Zen abdication and reforming — including the outline’s critical notes on speed, personnel, and missing “party” support for ideals.
Chapter 9 — Decay of unified government: Eastern Han
Tongyi zhengfu zhi duoluo; Donghan xingwang（統一政府之墮落；東漢興亡）
Eastern Han emperors and calendar; the imperial house; waizi (外戚, consort kin) and huanguan (宦官, eunuchs); how each group entered the throne’s body politic.
Chapter 10 — New place of the shi clans: rise of Eastern Han great houses
Shizu zhi xin diwei; Donghan mendi zhi xingqi（士族之新地位；東漢門第之興起）
Expanding political weight of shizu (士族); chaju (察举) and zhengbi (征辟) recruitment; Taixue (太学) and qingyi (清议, pure criticism); the danggu (党锢) proscriptions; how mendi (门第, great-family rank) hardens; manners of Eastern Han shi houses.
Chapter 11 — The unified government facing outward: Qin–Han power and foreign situations
Tongyi zhengfu zhi duiwai; Qin Han guoli yu duiwai xingshi（統一政府之對外；秦漢國力與對外形勢）
Compares Western and Eastern Han strength; Western Han and the Xiongnu (匈奴); Eastern Han and the Western Qiang (西羌).

Part IV — Wei, Jin, Northern and Southern Dynasties
Di si bian 第四编　魏晋南北朝之部
Chapter 12 — Long division begins: the Three Kingdoms
Changqi fenlie zhi kaishi; Sanguo shidai（長期分裂之開始；三國時代）
After Eastern Han breaks, the outline opens the long Wei–Jin–Nanbeichao decline: old court power fails, centrifugal warlords rise, new regimes stay dark, and thought finds no exit. Sanguo (三国) king-lists close the chapter as the start of multi-century split rather than a short heroic digression.
Chapter 13 — Afterglow of unified government: Western Jin
Tongyi zhengfu zhi huiguang fanzhao; Xijin xingwang（統一政府之迴光返照；西晉興亡）
Western Jin’s brief reunification is treated as afterglow, not recovery: weak throne, inland settlement of non-Han groups, capture of Huai and Min emperors, wreck of the old cultural centre, and entry of new religions as the unitary order finally dies.
Chapter 14 — New ground on the Yangtze: Eastern Jin southward
Changjiang liuyu zhi xin yuandi; Dongjin nandu（長江流域之新園地；東晉南渡）
With the north lost, the Yangtze basin becomes the main stage of “traditional China.” Eastern Jin king-list; repeated northern expeditions that never restore lasting unity; civil strife that eats the same energy that might have retaken the Central Plains.
Chapter 15 — Long northern chaos: Five Hu and Sixteen Kingdoms
Beifang zhi changqi fenluan; Wuhu shiliuguo（北方之長期紛亂；五胡十六國）
Tables and sketches of the Five Hu (Wuhu 五胡) and Sixteen Kingdoms: who settled where, how regimes succeeded one another, and the twin themes of sinicization and Hu–Han cooperation that the outline will carry into the Northern dynasties.
Chapter 16 — Southern dynasties sink: Song, Qi, Liang, Chen
Nanfang wangchao zhi xiaocheng; Nanchao Song Qi Liang Chen（南方王朝之消沉；南朝宋齊梁陳）
Southern Song–Qi–Liang–Chen king-lists; rotten courts and kin-killing; decline of southern mendi prestige. Against the north’s later recovery, the south is judged weaker in political vitality despite holding the cultural capital of the old elite.
Chapter 17 — New life for northern regimes: the Northern dynasties
Beifang zhengquan zhi xin shengming; Beichao（北方政權之新生命；北朝）
From Tuoba Wei through Eastern/Western Wei to Northern Qi and Northern Zhou: northern Han-ization and the Confucian scholarly line; Xiaowen’s (孝文) move of the capital; civil gains under Qi and Zhou that prepare Sui reunification.
Chapter 18 — Transformed feudal force: Wei–Jin–Nanbeichao mendi
Bianxiang de fengjian shili; Wei Jin Nanbeichao zhi mendi（變相的封建勢力；魏晉南北朝之門第）
Jiupin zhongzheng (九品中正) and great-family rank; decay of schools and open exams; southern immigrant qiaoxing (侨姓) versus native Wuxing (吴姓); marriage and status rules; northern junxing / guoxing (郡姓 / 国姓). Mendi (门第) is framed as a new quasi-feudal order after classical enfeoffment had already died.
Chapter 19 — Social form under that force (I): Western Jin and the south
Bianxiang de fengjian shili xia zhi shehui xingtai (shang); zai Xijin ji Nanchao（變相的封建勢力下之社會形態（上）；在西晉及南朝）
Late-Han desolation; changing farmer status; Western Jin household levies and official-rank land limits (guanpin zhantian 官品占田); southern immigrant great houses; soldiers’ legal status and burdens.
Chapter 20 — Social form under that force (II): Five Hu and the north
Bianxiang de fengjian shili xia zhi shehui xingtai (xia); zai Wuhu ji Beichao（變相的封建勢力下之社會形態（下）；在五胡及北朝）
Northern agrarian shares under the Five Hu; Northern Wei juntian (均田); Western Wei fubing (府兵) as institutional answers that later feed Sui–Tang machinery.
Chapter 21 — Spread of religious thought: antiquity through Northern–Southern Dynasties
Zongjiao sixiang zhi miman; shanggu zhi Nanbeichao zhi zongjiao sixiang（宗教思想之瀰漫；上古至南北朝之宗教思想）
Ancient cult change; Eastern Han Daojiao (道教) and recipe arts; Wei–Jin–Nanbeichao Buddhism; northern Dao–Buddhist clashes; a forward glance to Sui–Tang sinicization of Buddhist learning — religion as a structural mark of the long decline age.

Part V — Sui, Tang, Five Dynasties
Di wu bian 第五编　隋唐五代部
Chapter 22 — Unified florescence returns: Sui rise and fall; early Tang
Tongyi shengyun zhi zailin; Suishi xingwang ji Tang chu（統一盛運之再臨；隋室興亡及唐初）
Sui wealth, population, and granaries; Yangdi’s overreach; Tang founding and the Zhenguan (贞观) settlement as the second great unitary florescence after Qin–Han.
Chapter 23 — Political machinery under the new florescence: High Tang government
Xin de tongyi shengyun zhi xia zhi zhengzhi jigou; sheng Tang zhi zhengfu zuzhi（新的統一盛運之下之政治機構；盛唐之政府組織）
Rebuilding zaixiang (宰相) power after centuries of drift; refurbishing local government so the centre can again rule a whole empire without Wei–Jin style decay at the counties.
Chapter 24 — Social conditions under florescence: jinshi, fubing, and farmers
Xin de tongyi shengyun xia zhi shehui qingtai; sheng Tang zhi jinshi fubing yu nongmin（新的統一盛運下之社會情態；盛唐之進士府兵與農民）
Gongju (贡举) paths — pupils, prefectural tribute, decree exams — with jinshi (进士) supreme; zuyongdiao (租庸调) fiscal package; fubing (府兵) military households. Institutions read as the social face of High Tang strength.
Chapter 25 — Decay inside florescence (I): tax and military systems loosen
Shengyun zhong zhi shuai xiang (shang); Tangdai zushui zhidu yu bingyi zhidu zhi feichi（盛運中之衰象（上）；唐代租稅制度與兵役制度之廢弛）
When the spirit behind the rules fades, zuyongdiao slides toward liangshuifa (两税法); fubing yields to fangzhen (方镇) and palace armies. Institutional death is treated as loss of creating consciousness, not mere bad luck.
Chapter 26 — Decay inside florescence (II): officials and shi rot
Shengyun zhong zhi shuai xiang (xia); Tangdai zhengfu guanyuan yu shiren zhi fuhua（盛運中之衰象（下）；唐代政府官吏與士人之腐化）
Unlimited opening of office through exams and other doors; swelling of government posts; the same civil machinery that made florescence becomes overcrowded and soft.
Chapter 27 — Outward posture under florescence: early Tang arms and later threats
Xin de tongyi shengyun xia zhi duiwai zitai; Tang chu wugong ji zhongye yihou zhi waihuan（新的統一盛運下之對外姿態；唐初武功及中葉以後之外患）
Early success against Türks and other frontiers; the turn after An–Shi (安史) when foreign pressure and internal militarization reverse the High Tang external advantage.
Chapter 28 — A great age sinks: mid–late Tang politics and society
Da shidai zhi moluo; Tang zhongye yihou zhengzhi shehui zhi ge fangmian（大時代之沒落；唐中葉以後政治社會之各方面）
Fanzhen (藩镇) governors — often of non-Han origin — hold the provinces after An–Shi; the capital no longer commands the map. First half of the late-Tang diagnosis.
Chapter 29 — A great age sinks (continued)
Da shidai zhi moluo (xu)（大時代之沒落（續））
Palace eunuchs, court factions, and scholar-official party strife complete the internal picture: military provinces outside, closed and divided centre inside.
Chapter 30 — Dark shock: Huang Chao and the Five Dynasties / Ten Kingdoms
Hei’an shidai zhi da dongyao; Huang Chao zhi luan yiji Wudai shiguo（黑暗時代之大動搖；黃巢之亂以及五代十國）
Huang Chao (黄巢) and the fall of Tang; Wudai shiguo (五代十国); rise of the Khitan (Qidan 契丹); misery of the Central Plains; north–south split as structure again — the trough before Song recentralization.

Part VI — The two Song
Di liu bian 第六编　两宋之部
Chapter 31 — A poor-and-weak new centre: early Northern Song
Pinruo de xin zhongyang; Bei Song chuqi（貧弱的新中央；北宋初期）
Song king-list; rebuilding central power after the Five Dynasties; external weakness and internal poverty as paired structural traits; further institutional weak points that no early reform fully cures.
Chapter 32 — Literati self-awareness and reform: Qingli and Xining
Shidafu de zijue yu zhengzhi gexin yundong; Qingli Xining zhi bianfa（士大夫的自覺與政治革新運動；慶曆熙寧之變法）
Intellectual dawn among Song shi; Qingli (庆历) reforms; Xining (熙宁) New Policies under Wang Anshi (王安石) — reform as the self-conscious politics of a literati age.
Chapter 33 — Old and new party strife; northern and southern talents after Yuanyou
Xinjiu dangzheng yu nanbei rencai; Yuanyou yixia（新舊黨爭與南北人才；元祐以下）
New-party southern tilt; Luo–Shu–Shuo (洛蜀朔) opinion blocs; moral language of “upright vs wicked” that turns policy dispute into permanent faction war.
Chapter 34 — North–south split again: Song, Liao, and Jin war and peace
Nanbei zai fenlie; Song Liao Jin zhi hezhan（南北再分裂；宋遼金之和戰）
Jin destroys Liao; Jin destroys Northern Song; Southern Song–Jin war and peace; Southern Song finance; Liao / Jin / Song king-lists as scaffolding for the second long division of the millennium.

Part VII — Yuan and Ming
Di qi bian 第七编　元明之部
Chapter 35 — The storm arrives: Mongol conquest
Baofengyu zhi lailin; Menggu ruzhu（暴風雨之來臨；蒙古入主）
For Qian, the first time the whole country falls under a non-traditional alien regime. Steps against Xia, Jin, and Song; Yuan political climate; taxes and economic policy; armies and bans; clergy; scholars and the examination system under Mongol rule.
Chapter 36 — Traditional politics revived as monarchical dictatorship (I): Ming rise and fall
Chuantong zhengzhi fuxing xia zhi junzhu ducai (shang); Mingdai xingwang（傳統政治復興下之君主獨裁（上）；明代興亡）
Ming king-list; “worsening” of traditional politics into personal monarchy; abolition of the chancellorship; grand secretaries and eunuchs as the substitute centre.
Chapter 37 — Traditional politics revived as monarchical dictatorship (II)
Chuantong zhengzhi fuxing xia zhi junzhu ducai (xia)（傳統政治復興下之君主獨裁（下））
Early Ming “good institutions” and their later rot — the second half of the dictatorship diagnosis after the throne has already absorbed the old ministerial apex.
Chapter 38 — North–south transfer of economy and culture (I): Tang to Ming society
Nanbei jingji wenhua zhi zhuanyi (shang); zi Tang zhi Ming zhi shehui（南北經濟文化之轉移（上）；自唐至明之社會）
Economic and cultural maps; north–south political geography and population rise and fall — the opening block of the long transfer Lü Simian later praised.
Chapter 39 — North–south transfer (II)
Nanbei jingji wenhua zhi zhuanyi (zhong)（南北經濟文化之轉移（中））
Yellow River disasters in the north; damage from outside peoples and bad government that hollows the old heartland.
Chapter 40 — North–south transfer (III)
Nanbei jingji wenhua zhi zhuanyi (xia)（南北經濟文化之轉移（下））
Water control and development in Jiangsu–Zhejiang south — the constructive counterpart to northern decline, completing the Tang-to-Ming economic pivot.
Chapter 41 — Free private teaching rises again: Song–Yuan–Ming learning
Shehui ziyou jiangxue zhi zai xingqi; Song Yuan Ming sandai zhi xueshu（社會自由講學之再興起；宋元明三代之學術）
After aristocratic mendi fade, Song–Ming intellectual spirit, academies and lectures, and scholar-led social projects reopen a space of private teaching comparable, in Qian’s arc, to the pre-Qin masters.

Part VIII — Qing
Di ba bian 第八编　清代之部
Chapter 42 — “Narrow tribal regime” rebuilt (I): Qing entry
Xiayi de buzu zhengquan zhi zaijian (shang); Qingdai ruzhu（狹義的部族政權之再建（上）；清代入主）
Manchu rise to the pass (Jianzhou Jurchens, Nurhaci’s inherited armours, Seven Great Grievances, Ming military disaster); late Ming rebels; Southern Ming resistance — conquest as the return of a “narrow tribal” form of rule.
Chapter 43 — “Narrow tribal regime” rebuilt (II)
Xiayi de buzu zhengquan zhi zaijian (xia)（狹義的部族政權之再建（下））
Qing king-list; policy toward Han; institutions of the conquest regime; military expansion that secures the High Qing map.
Chapter 44 — Literati morale under that regime: scholarship before mid-Qing peak
Xiayi de buzu zhengquan xia zhi shiqi; Qingdai Qian–Jia yiqian zhi xueshu（狹義的部族政權下之士氣；清代乾嘉以前之學術）
Ming remnant integrity; Qian–Jia (乾嘉) philological climate; later divorce of politics from learning as morale and public purpose thin.
Chapter 45 — Popular upheaval under that politics: mid–late Qing disorders
Xiayi de buzu zhengzhi xia zhi minbian; Qing zhongye yixia zhi bianluan（狹義的部族政治下之民變；清中葉以下之變亂）
Peak-to-decline after Qianlong–Jiaqing; Hong–Yang / Taiping narrative under Qian’s own labels; Xiang and Huai armies and Tongzhi “restoration” as military answers that cannot fully reset the regime type.
Chapter 46 — Discard the old, open the new: Qing fall and Republican founding
Chu jiu yu kai xin; Qingdai fuwang yu Minguo chuangjian（除舊與開新；清代覆亡與民國創建）
Late Qing political scene; self-strengthening; abolition of keju (科举) and new schools; Wuxu (戊戌) and Xinhai (辛亥); post-1911 politics; cultural and social revolution; Sanmin zhuyi (三民主义) and war of resistance / national construction; closing vision of Chinese culture’s “new world mission” after victory — the outline’s wartime horizon, not a post-1949 continuation.

sources/jianguo-dagang-dengxiaoping-jich.content:
Theoretical Foundation of the Program of National Construction — A Study Companion to the Selected Works of Deng Xiaoping (Jianguo dagang lilun jichu 建国大纲理论基础——《邓小平文选》学习讲话) — Huang Zheng & Huang Hai 黄峥、黄海

Note on authorship. Despite the phrase 建国大纲 in the title, this is not a text by Sun Yat-sen and not his Jianguo dagang 建国大纲. It is a 1983 People’s Liberation Army party-study volume that treats Deng Xiaoping’s theory as the theoretical foundation (lilun jichu 理论基础) of the PRC’s program of national construction (jianguo dagang in its party-state sense), set against the Selected Works of Deng Xiaoping (《邓小平文选》). It belongs on the PRC / reform-era part of this shelf, alongside the republican-era Sun corpus as a later, contrasting stage of the same “建国” theme.

What this is
Huang Zheng and Huang Hai (黄峥、黄海 编) prepared this as an official-style study companion to the first volume of Deng Xiaoping’s Selected Works, issued by the PLA publishing house 战士出版社 in October 1983 (first edition, Nanjing first printing; 74,000 characters; print run 182,000; 157 PDF pages). It reads as party cadre educational material from the early reform era: eleven lectures walking through the main themes of the Selected Works, framed by a “代序” (surrogate preface) on why the Party’s policy shift under Deng was “a correct decision conforming to the necessary course of history.”
The work sits between two poles of recent Chinese history that it constantly references: the Cultural Revolution (文化大革命) and the Gang of Four (四人帮), which it treats as the disorder to be overcome, and the Third Plenum of the Eleventh Central Committee (十一届三中全会) and the Four Modernizations (四化), which it treats as the path forward. It defends Deng’s 1975 rectification (整顿) and rebuts the criticism of Deng / counterattack against right-deviationist reversal-of-verdicts campaign (批邓、反击右倾翻案风), while insisting on preserving Mao Zedong’s historical standing and continuing Mao Zedong Thought.

How it is organized
代序 — 符合历史发展必然的正确决策. Two epochal events from 1975 to the 12th Party Congress (1982): smashing the Gang of Four and ending the ten-year disorder of the Cultural Revolution; and the Third Plenum correcting “Left” errors and beginning comprehensive rectification of the reversal of verdicts. Locates Deng as a veteran revolutionary whose half-century of work serves the cause, in line with historical-materialist respect for the role of outstanding individuals.
第一讲 — 冲破教条主义和个人崇拜的禁锢，重新确立实事求是的思想路线. Breaking free of dogmatism and the cult of the individual; re-establishing the ideological line of seeking truth from facts.
第二讲 — 坚定不移地把党和国家的工作重点转移到经济建设上来. Unswervingly shifting the focus of Party and state work to economic construction.
第三讲 — 从中国特点出发、走中国式的现代化建设道路. Proceeding from China’s particular characteristics to take the Chinese-style road of modernization.
第四讲 — 尊重知识尊重人才，发挥知识分子在四化建设中的重要作用. Respecting knowledge and talent; giving intellectuals their important role in the Four Modernizations.
第五讲 — 改革政治体制和领导体制，建设高度的社会主义民主. Reforming the political and leadership systems; building a high level of socialist democracy.
第六讲 — 在建设高度物质文明的同时，建设高度的社会主义精神文明. Building a high level of socialist spiritual civilization alongside material civilization.
第七讲 — 发展和壮大革命的爱国统一战线. Developing and strengthening the revolutionary patriotic united front.
第八讲 — 建设强大的现代化正规化的革命军队. Building a powerful, modernized, regularized revolutionary army.
第九讲 — 坚持和改善党的领导，加强党的建设. Upholding and improving Party leadership; strengthening Party building.
第十讲 — 维护毛泽东同志的历史地位，坚持和发展毛泽东思想. Safeguarding Comrade Mao Zedong’s historical standing; upholding and developing Mao Zedong Thought.
第十一讲 — 学好《邓小平文选》，为开创社会主义现代化建设新局面而奋斗. Study the Selected Works of Deng Xiaoping well; strive to open a new situation in socialist modernization.
Content anchors (from OCR of the opening lectures)

1975年整顿. Lecture material opens on the year 1975 as “a page of history hard to forget” — grief, long-suppressed hope, and political storms. It describes how Mao, with Zhou Enlai ill, had Deng preside over daily central work, and how Deng made rectification (整顿) his guiding work principle — first the army, then industry, agriculture, commerce, culture-education, science-technology, and Party organization — fighting the Gang of Four “tit-for-tat but with strategy.” Eight of Deng’s pieces from this period are in the Selected Works.
批邓、反击右倾翻案风. The material recounts how Mao could not tolerate Deng systematically correcting Cultural Revolution errors and launched the “criticize Deng, counterattack the right-deviationist reversal-of-verdicts” campaign; the “three big poisonous weeds” (三株大毒草) — documents drafted from Deng’s guiding line such as《论全党全国各项工作的总纲》— circulated widely and, against the Gang’s intent, raised Deng’s prestige; April 1976 events followed.
Appraisal framing. Consistently treats 三中全会 as the turn, the Cultural Revolution as the negative pole to be overcome, and Deng’s line as historically necessary and correct — contemporary PLA study-doctrine voice, not an academic history.

Relation to the other sources
This is the first PRC-era source on this shelf. The three republican-era Sun sources (三民主义, 建国方略) present the revolutionary-nationalist program of 1924; this 1983 volume shows how a later party-state study text re-appropriated the vocabulary of 建国 and 现代化 in a Leninist–reform register. The title’s 建国大纲 echoes Sun’s, but the content is entirely post-1949 party history.

Plans for National Reconstruction (Jianguo fanglüe 建国方略) — Sun Zhongshan 孙中山
What this is
Sun Zhongshan (孙中山; also Sun Wen 孙文 / Sun Yat-sen) gathered under the umbrella title 建国方略 (Jianguo fanglüe, Plans for National Reconstruction) three major constructive programs written across the late 1910s and early 1920s — psychological reconstruction, material (industrial) reconstruction, and social (civic / parliamentary) reconstruction — together with a short 附编 of party-state foundational texts. Where the companion source 三民主义 (1924 Guangzhou lectures) states the Three Principles as public doctrine, 建国方略 is the how-to corpus: how to break the old “knowing is easy, doing is hard” mental block; how to build ports, railways, industry, and mines on an international-development scale; and how ordinary citizens are to run meetings so that “a sheet of loose sand” becomes organized public power.
This file is a 2012 simplified-Chinese ebook (AZW3 / Kindle MOBI lineage, chenjin5.com free-book imprint via Anna’s Archive). Body text is clean digital Chinese (not OCR of a scan). Commercial interstitial pages appear at the head of the package and do not cut the three main books.

Chapter breakdown
Style: English title + (pinyin + 中文) + multi-line content gloss grounded in this edition’s openings. Glosses track what the text argues in its own time, not later party doctrine.
Book I — Psychological reconstruction (Xinli jianshe 心理建设 / Sun Wen xueshuo 孙文学说)
Preface (Zixu 自序). Sun recounts thirty-odd years of running the national cause: the overthrow of Qing autocracy and founding of the republic should have opened onto the revolutionary party’s 三民主义, 五权宪法, and the construction templates of the older Geming fanglüe 革命方略. Instead, after the first success, party men called his claims “too idealistic” for China; as provisional president his influence was weaker than as revolutionary leader. Removing one Manchu autocracy produced “countless bandit autocracies,” worse for the people’s livelihood. He locates the intellectual disease in the proverb 知之非艰，行之惟艰 (“to know is not hard; to act is hard”) and announces the counter-thesis 行之非艰，知之惟艰 — doing is not hard; knowing is hard — as the key that unlocks construction.
Ch. 1 — Proof from eating and drinking (Yi yinshi wei zheng 以饮食为证). At the hinge from destruction to construction, critics invoke “knowing easy, doing hard.” Sun turns from Wang Yangming’s “unity of knowledge and action” to a long demonstration that everyone does diet every day while almost no one knows the chemistry, physiology, and hygiene of food — proof that action can be universal while knowledge remains rare and late.
Ch. 2 — Proof from using money (Yi yongqian wei zheng 以用钱为证). Money is not an innate faculty but a civilizational habit. All civilized people use it constantly, yet few can define what money is. Sun reviews Chinese and Western accounts of currency as medium and standard (“中准”), and the long history from cowries and metals to modern money — again, universal practice with scarce true knowledge.
Ch. 3 — Proof from composition (Yi zuowen wei zheng 以作文为证). Chinese civilization has exalted letters for millennia; ability in prose became a false universal competence while other arts decayed. Yet the script tradition is rich, durable, and assimilative (Japan, Korea, Vietnam as “同文”). New-learning proposals to abolish Chinese writing are rejected. Composition is something many do; grammar, rhetoric, and the science of language are things few know.
Ch. 4 — Proof from seven further matters (Yi qishi wei zheng 以七事为证). Extends the case beyond diet, money, and writing to building, shipbuilding, city walls, canals, electricity, chemistry, and evolution: crafts and sciences long practiced before theorized; foreign engineers design while Chinese laborers execute in the treaty-port landscape — knowledge and action divided among persons.
Ch. 5 — General theory of knowledge and action (Zhixing zonglun 知行总论). With ten proofs, the ancient “know easy, act hard” and Yangming’s “unity” are overturned as guides for national work. Mencius is cited for people who act and practice without understanding the Way. Yangming’s motive (urge people to do good) is granted; his formula still teaches fear of the hard and dampens action.
Ch. 6 — If one can know, one can act (Neng zhi bi neng xing 能知必能行). In a scientific age, large works (wireless, aircraft, continental railways, Suez and Panama) succeed when image, plan, and execution follow knowledge. Sun maps his own 革命方略 periods — 军政, 训政, 宪政 — as planned stages of destruction and construction once the doctrine is known.
Ch. 7 — One can act even without knowing (Bu zhi yi neng xing 不知亦能行). Objection: if science must come first, enrichment waits a century of schooling. Answer: most human advance begins in 不知而行 — drill, experiment, exploration, adventure. Scientific knowing is powerful but historically late; construction cannot wait for universal prior knowledge.
Ch. 8 — Where there is will, there is achievement (You zhi jing cheng 有志竟成). Affairs that match principle, popular feeling, world tide, and group need, once willed by the first to know, do not fail. Sun corrects earlier caution in Kidnapped in London and narrates the revolutionary origin from personal resolve through 兴中会 to 同盟会, overseas Chinese, and inland martyrs — memory as encouragement that construction too can be finished.
Book II — Material reconstruction (Wuzhi jianshe 物质建设 / Shiye jihua 实业计划)
Preface (Zixu 自序). Written as the European war ended: use wartime-scale machines and organized labor for China’s industrial leap and to absorb demobilized foreign labor. Powers instead demobilized industry; China lost a chance, while the world remained in economic distress. Development of China’s resources is a world problem; 发展之权，操之在我则存，操之在人则亡 — the right to develop, if held by us, means survival; if held by others, ruin.
Opening essay (Pianshou 篇首). Daily war expenditure and the “second industrial revolution” of state-scaled production leave surplus plant and labor when fighting stops. International joint development of China is framed as reconstruction for the powers and a path out of overproduction — the six plans follow.
Plan I (Di yi jihua 第一计划). Dual track: personal enterprise (encourage, legal protect, scrap suicidal taxes, fix currency, clear official barriers, ease transport) vs state enterprise for monopolistic or non-delegable works, using foreign capital and skilled organizers under training-for-succession terms. Four principles: most profitable routes for capital; what the people need most; least resistance; suitable location. Centers on a 北方大港 (Northern great port) and supporting systems (rail into the northwest, colonization, canals, iron/coal).
Plan II (Di er jihua 第二计划). 东方大港 (Eastern great port) as counterpart center — five parts: the eastern port (argument that a planned port on Hangzhou Bay near Zhapu outranks merely enlarging Shanghai), regulating the Yangzi waterway and banks, inland river ports, improving existing Yangzi routes and canals, and large cement works.
Plan III (Di san jihua 第三计划). 南方大港 at 广州 to complete the three first-class seaports: improve Guangzhou as world port; improve the Guangzhou water system; 西南铁路系统; coastal commercial and fishery ports; shipyards. Hong Kong’s rise after the Opium War is treated as having taken Guangzhou’s harbor role; republican “awakening” is to reverse that through Chinese public works.
Plan IV (Di si jihua 第四计划). Detail of the 100,000-mile railway vision: central, southeast, northeast, expanded northwest, and plateau systems, plus locomotive and rolling-stock works — knitting ports to interior and to Mongolian / Xinjiang / highland frontiers.
Plan V (Di wu jihua 第五计划). After key and fundamental industries, develop 本部工业 (consumer and comfort goods industries) so higher wages meet cheaper necessities and comforts; critiques the idea that China is a “cheap living” country when measured in labor hours rather than money.
Plan VI (Di liu jihua 第六计划). Mining as root of machine civilization: iron, coal, oil, copper, special minerals, mining machinery, smelting plants — government coordination of a still-young Chinese mining sector.
Conclusion (Jielun 结论). Three world problems — international war, commercial war, class war — are answered in this international development scheme through 互助 (mutual aid) rather than Darwinian struggle. Warns that China, as the most populous country, would again be the stake of great-power conflict if development is left to partition logic.
Appendices 1–6 (Fulu 附录). Supporting letters, documents, and technical notes attached to the industrial plan in this edition (international and engineering correspondence of the Shiye jihua dossier).
Book III — Social reconstruction (Shehui jianshe 社会建设 / Minquan chubu 民权初步)
Preface (Xu 序). China has the greatest people and richest land yet lagged Japan’s transformation because 人心涣散 — hearts scattered, strength uncondensed. Manchu bans on assembly, literary inquisition, and punishment for private talk stripped meeting, press, and thought freedoms for two and a half centuries. After foreign winds, Meiji example, and revolutionary shock produced the Republic, ambition still tried to restore empire (洪宪). The Republic’s safety now depends on developing 民权. Citing Lincoln’s government of/by/for the people, Sun presents this book as a primer of meeting procedure (after Western parliamentary practice) so four hundred million cease to be loose sand.
Juan 1 — Forming assemblies (Juan yi jiehui 卷一结会). Ch. 1–4: definition of a meeting (three or more under rules); need for officers and order versus the Chinese habit of unstructured talk; types (temporary meetings, committees, permanent societies); how to organize, elect, and keep records.
Juan 2 — Motions (Juan er dongyi 卷二动议). Ch. 5–10: the three-step spine of business — motion, debate, vote; six formal steps from rising and addressing the chair through announcement of the result; wording, seconding, withdrawal, division of questions, and related practice.
Juan 3 — Amendments (Juan san xiuzhengan 卷三修正案). Ch. 11–13: nature and effect of amendments; must be germane; primary/secondary amendment practice; ways to amend (insert, strike, substitute) with worked examples (e.g. a local self-government society hunting a hall).
Juan 4 — Order of motions (Juan si dongyi zhi shunxu 卷四动议之顺序). Ch. 14–18: independent vs subsidiary motions; seven common subsidiary motions and their precedence (including lay on the table, previous question / stop debate, commit, amend, postpone, etc.); privileged motions (adjourn, recess, questions of privilege).
Juan 5 — Questions of privilege and order (Juan wu quanyi ji zhixu wenti 卷五权宜及秩序问题). Ch. 19–20: points that interrupt ordinary motion order — privilege and order — when they may be raised, how the chair handles them, and limits (including relative to adjournment).
Conclusion and appendix. Closes the primer and adds model 章程, narrative illustrations of full meetings, and 表决 tables — teachable templates for societies and public bodies.
Supplement (Fubian 附编)
Manifesto of the First National Congress of the Chinese Kuomintang (Zhongguo Guomindang di-yi ci quanguo daibiao dahui xuanyan 中国国民党第一次全国代表大会宣言). Opens on China’s present: revolution from Jiawu through Gengzi to Xinhai overthrew monarchy but did not complete the passage from one-nation domination to multi-national equality, from autocracy to popular rights, from handicraft to capitalist production, or from semi-colony to independence. Diagnoses warlord and imperialist structure and states the reorganized party’s political program in the mid-1920s united-front setting.
National Government Outline of National Reconstruction (Guomin zhengfu jianguo dagang 国民政府建国大纲). Twenty-five articles: government builds the Republic on 三民主义 and 五权宪法; 民生 first (food, clothing, shelter, movement); then 民权 (election, recall, initiative, referendum under tutelage); then 民族 (domestic weak peoples to self-determination; resist foreign aggression and revise unequal treaties). Construction in three periods — 军政, 训政, 宪政 — with county autonomy as the unit, a constitution drafted after enough counties/provinces are ready, and final power in the people under five-yuan government.
Premier’s Testament (Zongli yizhu 总理遗嘱). Dated Minguo 14.2.24 (24 February 1925). Forty years for China’s freedom and equality; awaken the masses and unite with nations that treat China as equal; comrades must follow 建国方略, 建国大纲, 三民主义, and the First Congress manifesto; hasten a national assembly and abolition of unequal treaties. Signed 孙文.

Relation to the other Sun source
| | 三民主义 | This file 建国方略 |
|—|-------------------------------|---------------------------|
| Form | 1924 spoken lectures (16) | Treatises + procedure manual + party docs |
| Core | Doctrine of 民族 / 民权 / 民生 | Path of 心理 / 物质 / 社会 construction |
| Overlap | Shares 五权, 建国 stages, unequal treaties | 遗嘱 explicitly lists both works as binding guides |
Together they are the two legs of Sun’s late constructive corpus in this wiki: what the principles are, and how reconstruction is to be thought, built, and practiced in meetings.

sources/mao-zedong-xuanji-4vols.content:
Selected Works of Mao Zedong, Complete in Four Volumes (Mao Zedong xuanji 毛泽东选集) — Mao Zedong 毛泽东
What this is
《毛泽东选集》 (Mao Zedong xuanji, “Selected Works of Mao Zedong”) is the party-edited collection of writings by Mao Zedong (毛泽东), arranged by the periods of the Chinese Communist Party’s history and by date of composition. The four-volume arrangement here follows the standard editorial preface: Volume One holds writings from the First Revolutionary Civil War (第一次国内革命战争时期, the Great Revolution / united front with the Nationalists) and the Second Revolutionary Civil War (第二次国内革命战争时期, the agrarian revolution / Jiangxi Soviet and Long March years); Volumes Two and Three hold writings from the War of Resistance Against Japan (抗日战争时期); and Volume Four holds writings from the Third Revolutionary Civil War (第三次国内革命战争时期, the 1945–49 civil war through the founding of the PRC).
The editorial preface in this file records the standard provenance: earlier regional editions of the Selected Works were unauthorized, disorderly, and textually unreliable, and omitted important pieces; this selection was made chronologically, drawn more broadly to include works not in the local collections, and each piece was reviewed by the author, with some textual corrections and occasional additions or revisions. It notes the collection is still incomplete — because the Guomindang’s destruction of revolutionary documents and the dispersal of materials in the long wars meant not all of Mao’s works (especially many letters and telegrams) could be recovered. Certain once-popular works were excluded by the author’s wish (e.g. 《农村调查》), and others included only in part (e.g. only Chapter 1 of 《经济问题与财政问题》). The edition carries editorial notes (注释) — some of the “题解” kind attached to the first page of a piece, others political or technical, appended at the piece’s end.
The present file is an e-book (EPUB) rendering of the full four-volume set, with clean digital text. It is a large, authoritative-style source: the standard corpus of Mao’s selected writings from 1925 to 1949.
