How it is organized






























VolumeChinesePeriod covered第一卷第一次国内革命战争时期 · 第二次国内革命战争时期Great Revolution → agrarian revolution / Long March (1925–1937)第二卷抗日战争时期（上）War of Resistance, upper (1937–1940)第三卷抗日战争时期（下）War of Resistance, lower (1941–1945)第四卷第三次国内革命战争时期Civil war → founding of the PRC (1945–1949)
Chapter breakdown (by volume)
Style: English title + (pinyin + 中文) + short gloss of the major pieces. This is a large corpus; the breakdown names the anchor works of each period rather than every nav entry.
Volume 1 — The two revolutionary civil wars (第一卷)
First Revolutionary Civil War period. Opens with Mao’s early class analysis and the peasant movement:

中国社会各阶级的分析 (Analysis of the Classes in Chinese Society, Dec 1925) — “Who are our enemies? Who are our friends?”; analyzes landlord–comprador, middle (national bourgeois), petty-bourgeois, semi-proletarian, and proletarian classes; declares the industrial proletariat the leading force and the peasantry the closest ally.
湖南农民运动考察报告 (Report on an Investigation of the Peasant Movement in Hunan, Mar 1927) — the famous defense of the peasant associations’ revolutionary excesses (“糟得很” vs “好得很”), the vanguard role of the poor peasants, and the “fourteen great deeds” of the Hunan movement.

Second Revolutionary Civil War period. The Jiangxi Soviet and base-area classics:

中国的红色政权为什么能够存在？ (Why Is It That Red Political Power Can Exist in China?) and 井冈山的斗争 (The Struggle in the Jinggang Mountains) — the rationale and practice of the rural base areas and soviet regimes.
关于纠正党内的错误思想 (On Correcting Mistaken Ideas in the Party) — the Gutian Resolution, correcting purely military viewpoints, ultra-democracy, subjectivism, individualism, roving-rebel ideas, etc.
星星之火，可以燎原 (A Single Spark Can Start a Prairie Fire), 反对本本主义 (Oppose Book Worship — “no investigation, no right to speak”), and the economic/land pieces (必须注意经济工作, 怎样分析农村阶级, 我们的经济政策).
论反对日本帝国主义的策略 (On Tactics Against Japanese Imperialism, Dec 1935) — the Wayaobao speech on the national united front against Japan.
中国革命战争的战略问题 (Problems of Strategy in China’s Revolutionary War) — the strategic manual of revolutionary war.
实践论 (On Practice) and 矛盾论 (On Contradiction, 1937) — Mao’s two great philosophical essays, on the unity of knowledge and action and the law of contradiction, framing the party’s method.

Volume 2 — The War of Resistance, upper (第二卷)
The opening of the war against Japan:

反对日本进攻的方针、办法和前途 and 为动员一切力量争取抗战胜利而斗争 — the initial policy of total resistance.
论持久战 (On Protracted War, 1938) — the centerpiece strategy piece: refutes both the “national subjugation” thesis and the “quick victory” thesis; the three stages of the war; guerrilla and mobile war; “soldiers and civilians are the foundation of victory.”
抗日游击战争的战略问题 (Problems of Strategy in Guerrilla War Against Japan).
中国共产党在民族战争中的地位, 统一战线中的独立自主问题, 战争和战略问题 — party role, independence within the united front, and the primacy of armed struggle.
中国革命和中国共产党 (The Chinese Revolution and the Chinese Communist Party, 1939) — the survey of Chinese society and the nature of the Chinese revolution.
新民主主义论 (On New Democracy, 1940) — Mao’s systematic statement of “New Democracy”: a new-democratic political, economic, and cultural program distinct from both bourgeois dictatorship and socialism, and the assertion that China’s revolution is part of the world proletarian-socialist revolution.
纪念白求恩 (In Memory of Norman Bethune) and 《共产党人》发刊词 — the party-building pieces.

Volume 3 — The War of Resistance, lower (第三卷)
The rectification (整风) and later-war period:

改造我们的学习 (Reform Our Study), 整顿党的作风 (Rectify the Party’s Style of Work), 反对党八股 (Oppose Stereotyped Party Writing) — the core of the 1942–44 Yan’an Rectification Movement against subjectivism, sectarianism, and stereotyped writing.
在延安文艺座谈会上的讲话 (Talks at the Yan’an Forum on Literature and Art, 1942) — the definitive statement of art serving politics and the masses.
学习和时局 (Study and the Current Situation, 1944), 为人民服务 (Serve the People) — the famous commemorative piece on Zhang Side.
抗日时期的经济问题和财政问题 and the production-campaign pieces (组织起来, 必须学会做经济工作, 游击区也能够进行生产).
论联合政府 (On Coalition Government, 1945) — the 7th Congress political report, calling for a democratic coalition government.
愚公移山 (The Foolish Old Man Who Removed the Mountains) — the 7th Congress closing speech, the “two big mountains” of imperialism and feudalism.

Volume 4 — The Third Revolutionary Civil War (第四卷)
The 1945–49 civil war through the founding of the PRC:

抗日战争胜利后的时局和我们的方针 (The Situation and Our Policy After the Victory in the War of Resistance Against Japan, Aug 1945) — policy after Japan’s surrender; the role of Soviet entry in ending the war.
和美国记者安娜·路易斯·斯特朗的谈话 (Talk with the American Correspondent Anna Louise Strong, Aug 1946) — the “paper tiger” thesis (帝国主义和一切反动派都是纸老虎).
集中优势兵力，各个歼灭敌人 and the campaign-guidance pieces for the Liaoshen, Huaihai, and Pingjin campaigns (辽沈/淮海/平津战役作战方针).
目前形势和我们的任务 (The Present Situation and Our Tasks, 1947) — the Ten Great Military Principles and the new democratic economic program.
在中国共产党第七届中央委员会第二次全体会议上的报告 (Report to the Second Plenary Session of the Seventh Central Committee, Mar 1949) — the transition from countryside to cities, from revolution to construction.
论人民民主专政 (On the People’s Democratic Dictatorship, Jun 1949) — the theoretical statement of the new state, summing up 28 years of experience and the “lean to one side” line toward the Soviet camp.
丢掉幻想，准备斗争 (Cast Away Illusions, Prepare for Struggle), 别了，司徒雷登 (Farewell, Leighton Stuart), 为什么要讨论白皮书？, “友谊”，还是侵略？, 唯心历史观的破产 — the late-1949 polemics against the US “China White Paper” and Acheson’s account of modern China, defending the historical-materialist interpretation of the revolution.

Relation to the other sources
This is the first source by the leader of the Chinese Communist Party, and the chronological companion to the Nationalist-side materials:

























SourceSide / angle三民主義, 建国方略, 孫逸仙傳記, 大革命家孙逸仙Sun Yat-sen’s program and lives蒋介石日记 (1915–1949)The Nationalist leader’s own reflections (war, civil war, 1949)毛泽东选集 (this file)The Communist leader’s own writings (1925–1949)建国大纲理论基础 (1983)PRC-era party study re-appropriating the 建国 vocabulary under Deng
Where 蒋介石日记 gives Chiang’s first-person framing of the war, civil war, and defeat, 毛泽东选集 gives Mao’s first-person program, strategy, and theory on the other side — the two leaders’ texts as a matched pair across the 1925–49 revolutionary era, both carried forward in this wiki.
Source notes

Nature: Party-edited selected works — authorized by and reviewed by Mao, with editorial notes. It is a canonical source, not a neutral one: selection and annotation carry the official framing. Use it as contemporaneous CCP source text.
Language: simplified Chinese digital text; clean (high confidence).
Scope note: Covers 1925–1949 only (the four volumes here); Mao’s post-1949 writings are outside this collection.

sources/qingshigao-zhao-erxun.content:
Draft History of the Qing (Qingshi gao 清史稿)
Zhao Erxun (Zhao Erxun 趙爾巽 / 赵尔巽) and the Qing History Bureau (Qingshi guan 清史馆)
Republican draft dynastic history of the Qing house · standard 529 juan (volumes) · Chinese (classical historiographic prose)
EPUB digital object (2011 package; Anna’s Archive id in filename) · immutable extract wiki/raw/qingshigao-zhao-erxun.txt
Chinese names below are given in English or standard romanization first, with characters (and pinyin when helpful) in parentheses on first use in a section. Reign temple names keep the usual English forms (Kangxi, Qianlong, etc.) with Chinese once.

What this book is
This is the Qingshi gao (清史稿, Draft History of the Qing) — compiled under the Republican Qingshi guan (清史馆, Qing History Bureau), with Zhao Erxun (趙爾巽) as the name tradition attaches to the bureau’s work. It is not a private essay and not a finished zhengshi (正史, orthodox/standard history) certified by a later empire; the title itself marks a gao (稿, draft) dynastic history written in the received fourfold shape of the standard histories:

Benji (本纪, imperial annals)
Zhi (志, treatises on institutions and knowledge)
Biao (表, chronological and genealogical tables)
Liezhuan (列传, biographies and collective lives)

ending in long monographs on tusi (土司, native/aboriginal chieftaincies), fanbu (籓部 / 藩部, inner feudatories), and shuguo (属国, dependent/attached states).
A reader who has never opened the book will find, in Chinese of the official-historiographic register, a continuous account of the Qing as the bureau reconstructed it: how the Aisin Gioro (爱新觉罗) rose in the Jianzhou (建州) marches; how the Later Jin and then the Qing took the north and the Ming capital; how successive reigns ordered ritual, revenue, arms, law, and letters; how governors, banners, and feudatories staffed the realm; and how the house’s last generations met foreign residence, new offices, traffic by steam and wire, and the close of the imperial line under the Xuantong (宣统) emperor. The digital filing used here is a complete standard object of that draft — benji 25 + zhi 135 + biao 53 + liezhuan 316 = 529 juan — with continuous prose and tables through the spine, not a table-of-contents shell.
The present source page does not judge the bureau’s politics or later scholarly disputes over the draft. It narrates what the text contains, so that a reader without Chinese, and without the volumes open, can see the history the book itself lays out.

Scope and horizon
Beginning. The first annals open on the house before the dynastic name is settled: the Jianzhou (建州) setting, the Aisin Gioro line, and Taizu (太祖) Nurhaci (Nuerhachi 努尔哈齐). The body of the Taizu benji (太祖本纪) moves from the sexagenary year guiwei (癸未) — equated in the text with Ming Wanli 11 (明万历十一年, 1583) — when Nurhaci raises forces against Nikan Wailan (尼堪外兰) after the deaths associated with Tulun city (图伦城), through conquest and alliance among Jurchen groupings, the building of a capital and a banner order, and the proclamation of the Tianming (天命, “Heavenly Mandate”) era and a state that contemporaries and the draft treat as the foundation of the later Qing. Early pages are thick with place-names of the northeast, fortress takes, marriages, and the naming of the regime.
Middle. Through Taizong (太宗), Shizu (世祖), and the long High- and mid-Qing reigns the annals run year by year (or campaign by campaign) over accession, regency, war, disaster, sacrifice, personnel, and foreign or tributary contact. The treatises freeze institutions into topical monographs; the tables pin ranks, fiefs, and postings to time; the biographies multiply individual and grouped lives.
End. The last annals are the Xuantong huangdi benji (宣统皇帝本纪, Annals of the Xuantong Emperor). Late treatises include matter the older Twenty-Four Histories did not carry in the same form — jiaotong (交通, traffic and communications: posts, roads, steam, wire) and bangjiao (邦交, foreign intercourse with named states) — and the tables of jiaopin (交聘, diplomatic exchange / residencies) list resident envoys sent and received. The biographical division closes on model officials, scholars, writers, the loyal and the filial, recluses, artists, mathematical astronomers, women of note, then six juan of tusi, eight of fanbu, and four of shuguo.
A sample of Shuguo IV (属国四, Dependent States, juan 4) opens on the Gurkhas (Kuoerka 廓尔喀 — Nepal) relative to Ü-Tsang / Wei-Zang (卫藏, central Tibet as the draft names it), the absorption of Balbu (巴勒布) polities, and bounds toward Sikkim (Zhemengxiong 哲孟雄) and Bhutan (Bulukeba 布鲁克巴), then carries a heading-cluster of Central and Inner Asian names — among them Kokand (Haohan 浩罕), Burut / Kyrgyz (Bulute 布鲁特), Kazakh (Hasake 哈萨克), Andijan (Anjiyan 安集延), and others listed below under Dependent States — with narrative that includes late Qianlong-era conflict on the Tibetan frontier. The book’s object is the Qing dynasty in the bureau’s frame — not pre-Qin antiquity, and not Republican party politics after 1912, except where late annals, bangjiao, jiaopin, and shuguo touch the dynasty’s last external relations.

How the work is ordered
Like other standard histories, the draft does not tell one novel from page one to the end. It offers four concurrent instruments:

Benji (本纪) — the emperor’s reign as the spine of public time: accessions, edicts, campaigns, rites, portents, and the deaths and appointments the bureau thought belonged in the sovereign’s record.
Zhi (志) — systematic monographs on sky and calendar, geography, ritual and music, dress, examinations, offices, food and goods, rivers, war, law, literature, traffic, and foreign intercourse.
Biao (表) — compressed time-grids of empresses and consorts, imperial princes, banner and civil noble houses, Grand Council ministers, board presidents, governors-general and governors, frontier generals, feudatory genealogies, and diplomatic residencies.
Liezhuan (列传) — lives: first consorts and princes, then the long central run of officials and commanders, then classified terminal series and the three frontier/feudatory monographic blocks.

A single event (a war, a river breach, a treaty) may appear in the annals under its year, again in a treatise under its institution, again in a table as a posting, and again in the biography of a commander. The source page below follows the book’s own order so a reader can see what each large block is for.

Part I — Imperial annals (benji 本纪), 25 juan
The annals are twenty-five juan. They are not evenly thick: long reigns occupy several juan; short or late reigns may share or compress. What the reader meets is reign-ordered political narrative in classical annalistic style — not modern chapter essays.
Taizu (太祖) — Nurhaci (努尔哈齐)
The opening annals recount the pre-dynastic and dynastic founding of the house. After a genealogical and geographic preface (Jianzhou, the Aisin Gioro line, relations with Ming frontier structures), the narrative turns on guiwei (癸未) / Wanli 11 (万历十一年, 1583): Nurhaci’s rising against Nikan Wailan (尼堪外兰), the struggle over fortresses such as Tulun city (图伦城), the gathering of allies and the destruction of rivals among Jurchen groups, the organization of military following that becomes the Eight Banners (baqi 八旗) system, the choice of capitals, and the declaration of Tianming (天命) as era-name and of a state that the draft treats as the root of the Qing. The texture is names, places, marriages, submissions, and battles — the bureau’s origin story of the dynasty in the northeast before entry into China proper.
Taizong (太宗)
The Taizong annals continue state-building and external war after Nurhaci: further ordering of banners and offices, campaigns and negotiations toward Ming and toward Korean (Chaoxian 朝鲜) and Mongol theatres, and the transition of titles and capital practice that prepare the later entry into the Ming domains. The reader follows a conquest polity consolidating its claim to rule, still centered on the northeast and the steppe–Ming frontier, not yet the Beijing court of the later annals.
Shizu (世祖) — entry into the pass; Dorgon; early Qing at Beijing
The Shizu annals cover the reign of the emperor known in temple style as Shizu (the Shunzhi emperor in era-name usage): the moment the Qing take the Ming capital and begin to govern China proper. The prose carries the passage through the passes, the role of Dorgon (Duo’ergun 多尔衮) and other princes in regency and conquest, the installation of Qing rule at Beijing, the pursuit of Ming loyalist resistance in the south and along coasts and rivers, and the early settlement of banner garrisons, examinations, and metropolitan offices. For a reader, this is the hinge from a regional khanal-dynastic state to an empire seated on the Ming institutional map.
Shengzu (圣祖) — the Kangxi reign (Kangxi 康熙)
Several juan belong to the long Kangxi reign. The annals move year by year through minority and personal rule, the suppression of the Three Feudatories (sanfan 三藩) and related coastal and southern wars, campaigns toward Taiwan (Taiwan 台湾) and the maritime fringe, northern and northwestern war and treaty horizons (including the Russian frontier as the draft registers it), the ordering of the Yellow River (Huanghe 黄河) and Grand Canal (Dayunhe 大运河 / caoyun 漕运 system) as recurrent imperial concerns, literary and encyclopedic projects as they enter the court record, and the long management of princes, favorites, and succession. Disaster, eclipse, sacrifice, and personnel run in the same annalistic breath as war: the bureau’s Kangxi is a reign of consolidation after conquest, written as continuous sovereign time rather than as a modern thematic biography.
Shizong (世宗) — the Yongzheng reign (Yongzheng 雍正)
The Yongzheng annals are shorter in juan count than Kangxi or Qianlong but dense in administrative texture. They carry the succession after Kangxi, the emperor’s tightening of central document flow and secret memorial culture as the draft records it, fiscal and cadastral pressure, the handling of princes and cliques, northwestern and southwestern military and administrative pushes, and the moral-legal tone of edicts that later reigns inherit. A reader meets a reign framed as disciplinary reform of the conquest elite and the Han bureaucracy alike.
Gaozong (高宗) — the Qianlong reign (Qianlong 乾隆)
The Qianlong annals are among the thickest blocks in the benji. They run a very long reign: decades of campaigns the court counted among its major wars (western and southern fronts, Jinchuan (金川), Myanmar border affairs, Taiwan, Gurkha/Tibet, and others as the annals assign them), the incorporation and reordering of Huibu (回部, the Muslim/Tarim oasis regions in Qing administrative language) and other western spaces, enormous ritual and tour activity, literary inquisition and huge editorial projects as they appear in the sovereign record, favoritism and late-reign corruption crises, and the emperor’s abdication calendar in favor of the next reign while power still hangs on the retired emperor. Samples of mid-Qianlong years in the extract show the texture clearly: banner and Green Standard (lüying 绿营) transfers, river labor at Qingkou (清口) and related nodes, Korean and Ryukyu (Liuqiu 琉球) tributary missions, appointments across boards and provinces, and coded moral praise and blame of officials — the everyday machine of High Qing court time.
Renzong (仁宗) — the Jiaqing reign (Jiaqing 嘉庆)
The Jiaqing annals open a reign already under strain. The reader finds the death of Qianlong, the removal of late favorites, White Lotus (Bailian 白莲) and related uprisings and their suppression costs, piracy and coastal trouble, continued river and famine administration, and a court trying to restore order after the High Qing peak. The tone of the annals remains imperial and year-ordered; the content shifts toward internal unrest and fiscal fatigue.
Xuanzong (宣宗) — the Daoguang reign (Daoguang 道光)
Daoguang annals carry the dynasty into sharper foreign and fiscal pressure. Opium, maritime trade conflict, and the wars and settlements that follow appear in the sovereign record alongside ordinary personnel, rites, and disasters. Northwestern Muslim rebellions and other interior crises interleave with coastal diplomacy. For the reader of the draft, this reign is where “overseas” powers become a standing problem inside the annals, not only an item for later bangjiao treatises.
Wenzong (文宗) — the Xianfeng reign (Xianfeng 咸丰)
Xianfeng annals are dominated by the Taiping (太平) rebellion and concurrent northern and southern wars, the flight of the court when allied forces approach the capital, the new treaty regime, and the death of the emperor away from Beijing. Banner and provincial armies, irregulars, and the rise of Han provincial commanders enter the annals as the military ground shifts under the throne.
Muzong (穆宗) — the Tongzhi reign (Tongzhi 同治)
Tongzhi annals cover a child emperorship and regency under empresses dowager, the gradual suppression of Taiping, Nian (捻), and major Muslim rebellions, the early Self-Strengthening arsenals and offices as they appear in court time, and residual foreign residence and indemnity structures. The sovereign is often ceremonial in the prose; the political content sits in edicts, appointments, and campaign reports.
Dezong (德宗) — the Guangxu reign (Guangxu 光绪)
Guangxu annals run from another child accession through the empress dowager’s dominance, the Sino-Japanese war and its settlements, reform edicts and their reversal, the Boxer crisis and allied expedition, the late xinzheng (新政, “new policies”) program, and the emperor’s death. Institutional novelty — ministries on foreign models, schools, police, provincial consultative bodies — appears in the annals as appointments and edicts, and is expanded in the late zhiguan (职官, offices), xuanju (选举, selection/exams), jiaotong, and bangjiao treatises.
Xuantong emperor (Xuantong huangdi benji 宣统皇帝本纪)
The final annals are the Xuantong (宣统) reign: a child emperor, regency, continued new-policy restructuring, railway and constitutional crises as the draft records them, provincial separation, the 1911 uprisings, abdication edicts, and the close of Qing sovereign time. The reader finishes the benji not with Republican party history but with the bureau’s record of how the imperial line ends.
Across all twenty-five juan the method is the same: reign title + year, then compact entries. Modern chapter titles are rare; meaning is in the accumulation of campaigns, rites, floods, stars, and names.

Part II — Treatises (zhi 志), 135 juan
The treatises are the draft’s institutional memory. They do not replace the annals; they lift recurrent machinery out of year-time into topical monographs. Category counts in this filing follow the received Qingshi gao set.
Astronomy (tianwen 天文), 14 juan
These juan treat the sky as the bureau’s astronomical office recorded it: lunar and planetary mansions, polar and stellar divisions in Chinese uranography, anomalous appearances, and the link between heaven’s signs and the court’s obligation to observe and fix the calendar world. A reader finds technical star-and-sign prose, not a popular star myth book — continuous with earlier dynastic tianwen zhi (天文志).
Disasters and anomalies (zaiyi 灾异), 5 juan
A catalogue-treatise of earthquakes, floods, droughts, locusts, prodigies, and other disasters and omens, arranged so that the realm’s suffering and portents can be read apart from the annals’ year-entries. Useful to the bureau as moral-political weather; useful to a modern reader as a compressed disaster register across the dynasty.
Time and calendar systems (shixian 时宪), 9 juan
Shixian carries the calendar and mathematical-astronomical system of the Qing — the Shixian li (时宪历, “Timely Models” calendar) tradition and its underlying computational frames, including the engagement with Jesuit and later European methods as absorbed into official calendar work. The reader meets epoch constants, month-intercalation logic, and the institutional claim that correct time is a sovereign duty.
Geography (dili 地理), 28 juan
One of the largest treatise blocks. It lays out the Qing map in administrative language: metropolitan and provincial circuits, prefectures and counties, frontier generalships and dependency spaces, changes of name and seat across reigns, distances and bounds as the bureau fixed them. Reading it is like reading a dynastic gazetteer fused to a history of jurisdictional reform — from the early Qing inheritance of Ming units through High Qing expansion and late Qing new provinces and treaty-port scars as geography records them.
Rites (li 礼), 12 juan
Sacrifices at suburban altars and temples, ancestral rites, court ceremony, investiture, mourning, guest ritual, and the classification of ritual cases. The Qing claim to have ordered All-under-Heaven is written here as a code of performances the emperor and bureaucracy owe heaven, ancestors, and envoys.
Music (yue 乐), 8 juan
Court music, pitch standards, hymn texts, and the musical establishment — the aural half of ritual sovereignty. Instruments, modes, and institutional offices for music appear as historical monograph, including reform and antiquarian recovery across reigns.
Carriages and dress (yufu 舆服), 4 juan
Sumptuary and ceremonial regulation of vehicles, banners, crowns, robes, and rank marks — how status was made visible in motion and clothing for emperor, princes, officials, and others the code names.
Examinations and selection (xuanju 选举), 8 juan
The ladder of schools, exams, and alternative routes into office: keju (科举, civil service examination) sessions and tiers, special examinations, recommendation, purchase and contribution routes as the draft admits them, and late-Qing school and abroad-study channels that begin to displace the classical exam world. A reader sees both the High Qing exam monarchy and its late unraveling into “new education.”
Offices (zhiguan 职官), 6 juan
The tree of government: Grand Secretariat (neige 内阁) and Grand Council (junjichu 军机处), the Six Boards (liubu 六部) and their late successors, Censorate, banners and the Eight Banner offices, provincial governors-general (zongdu 总督) and governors (xunfu 巡抚), judicial and salt and grain posts, and the xin guanzhi (新官制, new official system) band that records late-Qing ministry reform. This is the prose map of who was supposed to do what, complementary to the personnel biao.
Food and goods (shihuo 食货), 6 juan
Land and population registration, taxes in kind and silver, tribute grain (caoliang 漕粮), salt, coinage and monetary troubles, warehouses, and related economic administration. For economic structure as the bureau understood it, these juan are the core monograph — always in the language of official supply and control, not of later economic theory.
Rivers and canals (hequ 河渠), 4 juan
The Yellow River, the Grand Canal, Huai (淮) and related systems, dikes, breaches, transport of tribute grain, and the offices of river administration. Recurrent catastrophe and repair from the annals are here systematized as hydraulic history.
Military (bing 兵), 12 juan
Eight Banners and Green Standard establishment, provincial armies and braves as they enter the official story, training, weapons, garrisons, military finance, and late new armies and navy fragments. The treatise form lets the reader see force structure apart from individual campaigns in the annals and lives in the biographies.
Law (xingfa 刑法), 3 juan
Codes, substatutes, punishments, revision across reigns, and judicial offices — the Qing legal order as a historical monograph, including the pressure of new crimes and foreign consular regimes at the end.
Bibliography (yiwen 艺文), 4 juan
A classified record of books and compilations the bureau attributed to the dynasty’s literary corpus — classics, history, masters, collections — in the tradition of dynastic bibliographical treatises. It is a map of titles and categories, not plot summaries of each work.
Traffic and communications (jiaotong 交通), 4 juan
A late-style treatise: routes, posts, shipping, railroads, telegraph and related infrastructure as the Qing state built, conceded, or regulated them. Together with bangjiao and late xuanju / zhiguan, this block marks the draft as a history that must absorb nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century material older standard histories never framed this way.
Foreign intercourse (bangjiao 邦交), 8 juan
Monographs of relations with named foreign states and groups as the bureau ordered them — not only the classical gong (贡, tribute) framework but treaty powers and neighbor states of the late empire. Read beside the jiaopin nianbiao (交聘年表, diplomatic residency year-tables) and the shuguo biographies, this is the draft’s external-relations encyclopedia.

Part III — Tables (biao 表), 53 juan
The tables are not narrative chapters. They are grids and genealogical streams that pin people and posts to time. A reader uses them to answer “who held what, when,” and “how a house or fief descended.”

Empresses and consorts (houfei biao 后妃表) — marital and rank chronology of the inner court.
Imperial princes (huangzi / zhuwang 皇子 / 诸王 related tables) — sons of emperors and princely lines as the bureau tabulated them.
Banner and noble houses (zhuchen fengjue shibiao 诸臣封爵世表) — hereditary ranks among meritorious and banner lineages across generations.
Grand Council ministers (junji dachen nianbiao 军机大臣年表) — year-ordered occupancy of the dynasty’s core executive council.
Board and metropolitan ministers (buyuan dachen nianbiao 部院大臣年表) — presidents and related high posts of the boards and courts, often in upper/lower (上/下) paired juan.
Provincial and frontier posts (jiangchen nianbiao 疆臣年表) — governors-general (including river and grain special posts), governors, and frontier generals, lieutenants, and high ministers of the marches.
Feudatory genealogies (fanbu shibiao 籓部世表) — ruling houses of inner feudatories in tabular descent.
Diplomatic residencies (jiaopin nianbiao 交聘年表) — two juan of the late pattern: Chinese envoys abroad and foreign envoys in China.

Grand secretaries (daxueshi 大学士) and coadjutors appear densely in annals and biographies even where a standalone daxueshi nianbiao (大学士年表) header is thin in the ebook navigation; entity work should read the junji and buyuan tables together with benji appointments rather than trusting the sidebar alone.

Part IV — Biographies (liezhuan 列传), 316 juan
The biographical division is more than half the book. It opens with the inner court and the blood elite, runs a vast central sequence of officials and commanders, then closes with moral and occupational categories and three monographic blocks on the non-prefectural periphery.
Consorts (houfei 后妃) — Liezhuan I (列传一)
Lives of empresses and consorts: family origin, rank rises and falls, motherhood of heirs, political intervention where the bureau records it, and death rites. This is the inner-court companion to the consort tables.
Princes (zhuwang 诸王) — Liezhuan II–VIII (列传二–八)
Seven juan of imperial princes and princely houses — merits in conquest, fiefs, scandals, degradations, and branches of the Aisin Gioro and associated lines. Early juan lean on founding brothers and sons; later material tracks enfeoffed lines through the dynasty.
Central run of officials and commanders — roughly Liezhuan IX through the low 260s
Here the draft stacks individual and grouped biographies in the bureau’s sequence: early conquerors and collaborators, High Qing grand secretaries and generals, mid-Qing administrators, suppression commanders of the nineteenth century, statesmen of Self-Strengthening and reform, and figures of the close. Many mid-juan have only bare Liezhuan N labels in the ebook nav; inside the prose, lives are person-titled. The language of the corpus also knows condemnatory or liminal classes — erchen (贰臣, officials who served two dynasties), nichen (逆臣, rebellious ministers), jianchen (奸臣, treacherous ministers), panchen (叛臣, turncoat ministers) and related labels — used when the bureau sorts moral types; exact juan cuts for those labels should be fixed when those fascicles are opened for entity pages. For a reader, this long middle is the human grain of Qing government and war: not one plot, but hundreds of careers that together enact the annals.
Model officials (xunli 循吏)
Several juan of officials praised for upright local administration — the draft’s gallery of “followable officials,” useful as the bureau’s ideal of governance rather than as a statistical sample of all magistrates.
Confucian scholars (rulin 儒林)
Lives of classical scholars and intellectual lineages as the bureau recognized them — evidential research, school affiliation, works, and official or teaching careers.
Literary figures (wenyuan 文苑)
Writers and literary reputations: poets, prose masters, and men of letters whose fame the draft places under letters rather than under pure official merit.
Loyalty and righteousness (zhongyi 忠义)
A long block (on the order of ten juan) of those who died or suffered for loyalty — especially thick for conquest, Ming–Qing transition, and nineteenth-century wars and rebellions. Collective entries and local mass deaths appear beside famous names.
Filiality and duty (xiaoyi 孝义)
Exemplars of filial piety and kindred virtues — moral biography continuous with earlier dynastic histories’ didactic collections.
Remnant recluses (yiyi 遗逸)
Men who withdrew or refused service — including tones of Ming remnant loyalty and later eremitic choice — as the bureau chose to remember them.
Arts (yishu 艺术)
Painters, calligraphers, physicians, and other technical-artistic lives that sit outside the pure scholar-official ladder.
Mathematical astronomers (chouren 畴人)
Specialists in calendar, calculation, and related exact knowledge — a thin but pointed continuation of the chouren tradition, to be read beside shixian and tianwen.
Women (lienü 列女)
Four juan of women exemplary for chastity, martyrdom, talent, or other virtues the bureau’s category admits — a didactic female companion to zhongyi and xiaoyi.
Aboriginal offices (tusi 土司), six juan
Not brief epitaphs but a regional-administrative monograph series: native chieftaincies of the southwest and related zones, their genealogies, submissions, rebellions, and conversion toward direct rule (gaitu guiliu 改土归流, replacing native chieftains with circulating appointed officials) as the draft narrates it. Geography and surname-polities dominate.
Feudatories (fanbu 籓部), eight juan
Inner Asian and related feudatory polities under Qing suzerainty — Mongol leagues and khans, Tibetan and other highland structures as classified here, and the institutional story of titles, tribute, and intervention. Read with fanbu shibiao and dili.
Dependent states (shuguo 属国), four juan
The outer ring of “attached states” in the bureau’s language. Earlier shuguo juan treat long-standing partners as the bureau ordered them — notably Korea (Chaoxian 朝鲜), Ryukyu (Liuqiu 琉球), Vietnam (Annan / Yuenan 安南 / 越南), and related Southeast and East Asian partners where the draft places them.
Shuguo IV (属国四, Dependent States, juan 4) in this extract is especially thick on the Himalayan and Central Asian rim. It opens on:

What a continuous reader learns (without reading every juan)
Taken as one bureau project, the Qingshi gao offers:

A sovereign-time history of the Qing from Nurhaci’s rise and the Tianming (天命) state to the Xuantong (宣统) abdication, in annalistic grit rather than modern chapter synthesis.
An institutional encyclopedia of how the dynasty claimed to know heaven and time, map territory, stage ritual, recruit officials, tax and move grain, fight, punish, print and classify books, lay rails and wires, and deal with foreign states.
A personnel machine in tables: who sat on the Grand Council, who governed provinces, how noble and feudatory houses descended.
A biographical nation: consorts, princes, the working elite, moral exemplars, specialists, women of the didactic categories, and the native (tusi), feudatory (fanbu), and dependent (shuguo) peripheries.

It does not replace local gazetteers, private memoirs, archival streams, or foreign-language sources; it is the late, official-style summa of the dynasty written after the dynasty fell, in the shape of the standard histories.

Completeness of this digital object
Complete as a standard Qingshi gao filing: all four divisions are present at the received counts (25 + 135 + 53 + 316 = 529). The extract is on the order of 5.3 million characters of continuous classical prose and tables; spine documents are non-empty. Narrative is verified at the founding end (Taizu / Tianming arc) and in late matter (Xuantong annals present; shuguo with real monograph texture). Late treatises (jiaotong, bangjiao, xin guanzhi inside offices, jiaopin tables) confirm the object runs through the dynasty’s final institutional layer.
Caveats (properties of the work or the package, not silent truncation):

Gao, not zhengshi (稿, not 正史) — a Republican bureau draft; unfinished certification is in the title.
Ebook navigation is thinner than the body — many zhi juan and most mid-liezhuan lack human titles in the NCX; content remains in the raw extract. Do not treat missing sidebar labels as missing juan.
Orthography — mixed modern simplified/traditional typesetting typical of digital Qingshi gao packages; not a diplomatic transcript of one 1928 print copy.
Secondary directory residue near the file end is navigation debris, not a second incomplete book.

Bottom line: fit foundation source for Qing-wide work in this wiki. It does not by itself cover pre-Qing antiquity or post-imperial politics except where late external-relations matter touches them.

Note on this page’s method
Earlier draft of this source page leaned on division counts and category tables (imperial annals / treatises / tables / biography labels). That scaffolding is true but not what a reader needs first. Following the Rest of Europe 1800–65 pattern (e.g. German and Russian multi-volume sources), this page narrates the contents in English: what each large block of the book actually walks through, with concrete anchors from the extract (guiwei / Wanli 11 and Nikan Wailan; Dorgon and entry into the pass; mid-Qianlong year-texture; shixian and bangjiao/jiaotong as institutional horizons; Shuguo IV on Gurkha/Nepal and Central Asian names). Chinese characters remain where they identify the source’s own labels; they are paired with romanization and, where stable, common English names so a non-reader of the book is not left with untranslated strings. Three Principles of the People (Sanmin zhuyi 三民主義) — Sun Wen 孫文
What this is
Sun Wen (孫文; Sun Yat-sen / 孫中山) delivered these lectures at Guangzhou in Minguo 13 (民國十三年 / 1924) as a systematic public statement of the Three Principles of the People (Sanmin zhuyi 三民主義): nationalism (minzu zhuyi 民族主義), democracy / people’s rights (minquan zhuyi 民權主義), and people’s livelihood (minsheng zhuyi 民生主義). The present file is a collector’s edition (diancang ban 典藏版) PDF titled 三民主義(典藏版) — 孫文 — 2003 — a blue hardbound-style scan of the lecture corpus with portrait front matter, calligraphy preface page, table of contents, and the full run of lectures through the fourth minsheng lecture.
The work is not a dynastic narrative history like the companion 清史稿 / 国史大纲 / 中国通史 sources. It is a programmatic political-thought text: definitions, world comparisons, and policy claims aimed at party cadre and public audiences in the mid-1920s Guangzhou context. The 民生 series stops at four lectures in the published set — the corpus ends where the spoken series left off, not with a later PRC-era continuation.

Chapter breakdown (lecture-by-lecture)
Style: English title + (pinyin + 中文) + multi-line content gloss grounded in this edition’s openings / TOC / OCR body. Glosses track what the lecture argues, not later party doctrine.
Front matter
Portrait and seals. Guofu yixiang 國父遺像 and decorative endpapers frame the volume as a commemorative diancang object, not a bare lecture reprint.
Author’s preface (Zixu 自序). Dated 民國十三年三月三十日 at the Guangzhou Grand Headquarters (Guangzhou dabenzhen 廣州大本營). Sun presents the lectures as a corrected, extended textbook for comrades after earlier drafts and gaps; seals and calligraphy close the leaf. Positions the book as teaching material for the party’s nationalist program rather than as a finished philosophical system.
民族主義 — Nationalism
1. Nationalism, first lecture (Minzu zhuyi di yi jiang 民族主義第一講). 1924-01-27. Opens by defining ism as thought, belief, and force, and 三民主義 as 救國主義 (a doctrine to save the country). Equates Chinese minzu zhuyi with 國族主義 (nation-ism): China has family and clan loyalty but weak nation-group consciousness. Distinguishes 民族 (formed by natural “kingly way” forces) from 國家 (formed by coercive “hegemonic” force). Lists blood, livelihood, language, religion, and customs as natural binders of peoples; surveys world population pressure on China.
2. Nationalism, second lecture (di er jiang 第二講). 1924-02-03. Presses population and natural selection themes: nations rise and fall with numbers; China faces simultaneous political and economic oppression from the powers. Develops the claim that foreign banks, shipping, concessions, indemnities, and trade structure drain Chinese wealth year by year. Argues that loss of political power enables permanent economic drain — the double pressure that motivates nationalist revival.
3. Nationalism, third lecture (di san jiang 第三講). 1924-02-10. Turns to Manchu conquest methods and comparative foreign rule: how alien dynasties held China, and how that history should shape Han/Chinese national consciousness without simple revenge politics. Discusses Qing techniques of control and the need to rebuild national spirit after long subject status. Bridges historical subjugation to the present unequal-treaty order.
4. Nationalism, fourth lecture (di si jiang 第四講). 1924-02-17. Widens to world nationalism and the post–World War scene: self-determination rhetoric, the status of weak nations, and China’s place among them. Contrasts European national movements with Asian conditions. Urges Chinese nationalism as recovery of equal standing among states, not isolation.
5. Nationalism, fifth lecture (di wu jiang 第五講). 1924-02-24. Focuses on method: how to restore nationalism after it was “lost” under Qing cosmopolitan empire and treaty-port culture. Family and clan organizations as usable building blocks for larger national solidarity. Moral and organizational means — not only military force — for national revival.
6. Nationalism, sixth lecture (di liu jiang 第六講). 1924-03-02. Closes the nationalism series with cosmopolitanism vs nationalism, traditional Chinese moral claims (including datong language), and the duty of a revived China toward the world. Warns against abandoning nationalism too early under the slogan of world unity. Ends the first principle’s arc: recover the nation, then talk of broader harmony.
民權主義 — People’s rights
1. People’s rights, first lecture (Minquan zhuyi di yi jiang 民權主義第一講). 1924-03-09. Defines 政 as the affairs of the multitude and 治 as management; 民權 as the people’s power over that management. Sketches ages of struggle — man vs beast, man vs nature, man vs man — ending in the age of popular rights. Introduces democracy as the modern form of that struggle and begins comparing Chinese and Western political experience.
2. People’s rights, second lecture (di er jiang 第二講). 1924-03-16. Centers freedom: European history fought for liberty against feudal and clerical bonds; Chinese historical pain was less “unfreedom” in the European sense than loose sand disunity and later imperial/treaty oppression. Argues China should not copy Europe’s freedom slogan blindly; the need is effective national organization. Distinguishes personal license from political capacity.
3. People’s rights, third lecture (di san jiang 第三講). 1924-03-23. Centers equality: natural vs artificial equality; critiques flat equality that ignores ability. Develops the three types of people by talent (discoverers, promoters, operators) and the idea of service rather than class war as the moral of unequal gifts. Ties equality of political standing to unequal functions in administration.
4. People’s rights, fourth lecture (di si jiang 第四講). 1924-04-13. Reviews Western democracy’s progress and failures — revolutions, constitutions, party machines, and the gap between popular sovereignty in name and elite control in practice. Uses American and European examples to show where pure copied forms stall. Prepares the ground for a Chinese institutional redesign rather than simple transplant.
5. People’s rights, fifth lecture (di wu jiang 第五講). 1924-04-20. Presents the separation of power and capacity (quan neng fenshe 權能分開): the people retain four political powers (election, recall, initiative, referendum); the government exercises five governing powers (executive, legislative, judicial, examination, control) — the 五權憲法 frame. Machinery metaphors: popular control without crippling administrative competence. Core institutional lecture of the minquan series.
6. People’s rights, sixth lecture (di liu jiang 第六講). 1924-04-26. Completes the machinery discussion: how the five-power government and four popular powers mesh in practice, and how China might move from military/tutelage stages toward constitutional rule. Reinforces trained government plus sovereign people against both monarchic residue and chaotic mass politics. Closes the second principle.
民生主義 — People’s livelihood
1. People’s livelihood, first lecture (Minsheng zhuyi di yi jiang 民生主義第一講). 1924-08-03. Defines 民生 as the people’s life — food, clothing, shelter, movement — and as the center of social history. Positions minsheng against both uncritical Marxism and pure laissez-faire; discusses Marx, surplus value, and whether materialist class war fits Chinese conditions. Opens land and capital as the two great livelihood problems.
2. People’s livelihood, second lecture (di er jiang 第二講). 1924-08-10. Develops land policy: equalization of land rights (pingjun diquan 平均地權), value capture on unearned increment, and urban/rural land problems. Contrasts China’s still-limited industrial capitalism with Europe’s. Argues preventive regulation so China need not repeat Western social rupture.
3. People’s livelihood, third lecture (di san jiang 第三講). 1924-08-17. Turns to food (chifan 吃飯): agriculture, farmer livelihood, transport, and national planning for subsistence. Treats food as the first livelihood test of government. Links rural production to the wider minsheng program and to political sovereignty over economy.
4. People’s livelihood, fourth lecture (di si jiang 第四講). 1924-08-24. Centers clothing and related industrial chains (silk, cotton, wool, leather): why Chinese textile and filament industries fail under foreign political-economic pressure, tariffs, and unequal treaties. Calls for state-scale planning, customs recovery, and protection of raw and finished goods. Ends the published lecture series on industrial-political remedies for livelihood; no fifth/sixth minsheng lectures appear in this complete standard set.
Years covered

Spoken/written core: Minguo 13 (1924), Guangzhou — January through August lecture dates as above; preface 30 March 1924.
Historical references inside the text: late Qing defeats and indemnities, unequal treaties, treaty ports, comparative notes on Europe, America, Japan, Russia, and Asian peoples — used as argument, not as continuous chronicle.
This physical edition: 2003 collector’s reprint/scan branding in the filename; content remains the 1924 lecture canon.
Not covered: post-1925 institutional history of the KMT state, wartime revisions, or PRC reinterpretations — those are outside this source’s voice.

What this is
孫逸仙傳記 (Sun Yixian zhuanji, “Biography of Sun Yat-sen”) is a translated biography of Sun Yat-sen (孫文 / 孫中山; here 孫逸仙) issued as a volume of the 中國國民黨叢書 (Collection of the Chinese Nationalist Party / Kuomintang series). The translator is 徐植仁 (Xu Zhiren), and the volume was published by the 中國文化服務社 (China Cultural Service Agency; 發行人 劉百閔) with an editorial preface to the party series. This is a translation of an original Western-authored biography of Sun — the narrative voice is that of a foreign observer describing China and Sun from the outside (Guangdong as a land of lively Cantonese, Sun as “the child who created the Republic of China”), and the chapter set traces Sun from his 翠亨 village childhood through the fall of the Qing to his 1925 death.
The 1946 imprint records 中華民國三十二年十月 再版 (second printing, October 1943) and 中華民國三十五年一月 再一版 (reissue, January 1946). The cover sheet carries the series title and 孫逸仙傳記, with 譯者 徐植仁. The preface (敘言) is signed 葉楚傖, dated 三二九 (29 March).

Chapter breakdown (period by period)
Style: English title + (pinyin + 中文) + multi-line content gloss grounded in the TOC and body openings. Glosses follow the biography’s own framing as a foreign observer’s account.
Front matter
Series preface (敘言). The Kuomintang series editorial (signed 葉楚傖) explains the purpose of the 中國國民黨叢書: to preserve the party’s revolutionary history and its leaders’ doctrine — from 興中會, 同盟會, 國民黨, 中華革命黨 to 中國國民黨 — and to rally national confidence in 三民主義 under the 總理 and 總裁 (Chiang Kai-shek), amid the simultaneous war of resistance and national construction. It states the series gathers party-historical documents, the leaders’ revolutionary theory and pronouncements, and foreign scholars’ writings that spread the party’s doctrine.
第一期 — Early life in China (早年中國生活, 1866–1889)
Sections 一–十八 describe Sun’s childhood and boyhood.
一 翠亨 (Cuìhēng). Opens with Sun’s native village 翠亨 under a hill in Guangdong — birthplace (the narrative dates his birth 1866, 民國紀元前四十六年, 清同治丙寅十月初六) of “the child who created the Republic of China.” The village’s free, independent spirit and its nearness to Canton and Macao formed Sun’s temperament; an aunt’s tales of foreign ships and a returned overseas merchant’s stories of a golden land beyond the sea stirred his early resolve to study the foreigners.
二 廣東第一 (Guangdong first). A portrait of Guangdong as the southernmost of the eighteen provinces — its wealth, its lively, intelligent, enterprising Cantonese, its overseas communities, and the temperament Sun drew from the region. The biography repeatedly credits Guangdong’s people and émigrés with supporting his revolutionary work.
三–五 正直的父親 / 賢莊的母親 / 命名和住址 (The upright father; the worthy mother; naming and address). Family portraits: Sun’s father as a sober village man, his mother as the anchor of the household, and the naming and circumstances of Sun’s early home.
六–八 幼年的遊戲 / 中山和三字經 / 水災的故事 (Childhood games; Sun and the Three Character Classic; the story of the flood). Sun’s early schooling (including the 三字經 primer), his games, and formative village stories — including a tale of how one hoards treasure against flood and robbery, which Sun took as a practical lesson about the world of taking and keeping.
九–十一 官吏和三個有錯的弟兄 / 白契 / 幼年的搜求真理者 (The official and three erring brothers; the blank deed; the young seeker after truth). Village encounters with officialdom, corruption, and injustice that turned the young Sun’s mind toward truth-seeking and reform.
十二–十四 中山對於改造的第一次努力 / 徑奴中的人們 / 中國就是天下 (Sun’s first effort at reform; the people in bondage; China is the world). Sun’s first attempts at social change — including his boyhood protest against foot-binding for his sister, which the book marks as his first reform act — and observations on village servitude and China’s old conviction that China is “the world.”
十五–十八 大可 / 大哥從火奴魯魯回來 / 饋贈的教訓 / 從海港所得的教訓 (Dake; the elder brother returns from Honolulu; the lesson of gifts; the lesson from the harbor). Family and village episodes, including the return of Sun’s elder brother from Honolulu (a link to his later Hawaiian journey) and lessons drawn from gifts and the harbor at 金星港.
第二期 — Sojourn in Honolulu (在火奴魯魯旅居生活, 1879–1883)
Sections 十九–二十: 火奴魯魯 (Honolulu) and 在夏威夷商務和學校中的時代 (the age of business and school in Hawaii). Sun joins his elder brother, works and studies in the Hawaiian commercial and school setting, and is exposed to Western education and Christianity.
第三期 — Sojourn in Hong Kong (在香港的旅居, 1884–1886)
Sections 二十一–二十五: 皇家的營糧農; 在翅味鄉村中的宣傳工作 (propaganda work in the village); 中山與耶穌教徒的神像 (Sun and the Christians’ images); 皇仁學校裡的英國勢力、中法之戰的一天 (British influence at the Royal School / Queens College; the day of the Sino-French War); 不愛錢 (not loving money). Sun’s Hong Kong schooling, his engagement with Christianity, and the impact of the Sino-French War (中法戰爭) on his thinking.
第四期 — Sun’s profession (中山的職業, 1886–1894)
Section 二十六 職業的選擇、醫學校、宣告獨立、革命死了 (Choosing a profession; the medical school; declaring independence; the revolution dies). Sun’s choice of medicine, his medical studies, and the transition from doctor to revolutionary — the moment his medical career gives way to politics.
第五期 — Early revolutionary life (初期革命生活, 1895–1896)
Section 二十七 第一次懸賞購中山頭、倫敦使館遇難 (The first reward offered for Sun’s head; the London Legation incident). The first bounty on Sun’s head and the celebrated London kidnapping (倫敦被難) at the Chinese legation in 1896.
第六期 — Urgent revolutionary methods (迫切革命方法, 1896–1911)
Sections 二十八–三十二: 山下區一百二十哩; 中山與勞工 (Sun and labor); 演說家的中山、鎮靜的中山、寬想的中山 (Sun as orator, calm, broad-minded); 中山與黃馬; 牢記你到芝加哥去的時光 (remember the time you went to Chicago). Sun’s world tours, his organizing among overseas Chinese and labor, and the propaganda and fundraising that built the pre-1911 revolutionary movement.
第七期 — The provisional presidency (臨時總統任期, 1912–1913)
Sections 三十三–三十四: 中華民國的第一個大總統 (the first provisional president of the Republic of China) and 袁世凱的陰謀 (Yuan Shikai’s intrigues). Sun’s inauguration and the maneuvering by which Yuan Shikai succeeded him.
第八期 — Revolution after the provisional presidency (臨時總統後之革命, 1913–1916)
Section 三十五 袁世凱的末路 (Yuan Shikai’s end). The fight against Yuan — the second revolution (二次革命) and the campaign against the monarchist restoration.
第九期 — Life in Shanghai (在上海的生活, 1916–1918)
Sections 三十六–三十九: 中山對於美國的機會 (Sun’s opportunities toward America); 中山法中的瘋人; 中山的家庭生活（在上海莫利愛路的家） (Sun’s family life at his Moulieux Road home in Shanghai); 結論、中山的主義 (Conclusion: Sun’s doctrine). Sun’s Shanghai years, his writings, and the concluding statement of his 主義.
第十期 — The late revolutionary period (晚年革命時期, 1921–1925)
Sections 四十–四十七: 組織新政府被舉為總統 (organizing a new government and being elected president); 廣州避難 (taking refuge in Guangzhou); 拒絕北上 (refusing to go north); 三民主義宣言 (the Three Principles proclamation); 為什麼離廣州 (why he left Guangzhou); 處置革命之商園; 聯俄 (alignment with Soviet Russia); 逝世 (his death, 1925). The final decade: the Canton governments, the Three Principles, the alliance with Soviet Russia, and Sun’s death.

What this is
《置身事内：中国政府与经济发展》 (Zhishen shi nei, “Inside the Game: The Chinese Government and Economic Development”) is a contemporary work of political economy by 兰小欢 (Lan Xiaohuan), a professor at 复旦经济学院 (Fudan University School of Economics), published by 上海人民出版社 (Shanghai People’s Publishing House) in 2021. It is a widely-read analysis of how the Chinese government and economy interact, written for a general audience, drawn from his teaching.
The book’s argument, in its own framing, is that no serious analysis of the Chinese economy can leave out the government — one must “get inside the game” (置身事内) rather than stand outside it. It explains the micro-mechanisms by which local governments finance, invest, and drive development, and then the macro-phenomena (urbanization, debt, external imbalance) that follow. It is a contemporary source on the PRC’s political economy in the reform era, reflecting the state of Chinese economic thinking at the start of the 2020s.

前言 — From understanding the present (从了解现状开始)
Frames the method: to understand China’s development one must start from how things actually work today, and crucially not leave out the government. Sets up the “inside the game” (置身事内) premise.
Part 1 — Micro mechanisms (上篇 微观机制)
第一章　地方政府的权力与事务 (Local government: power and affairs). How Chinese local government works: the characteristics of government governance (政府治理的特点); externality and economies of scale (外部性与规模经济); complex information (复杂信息); incentive compatibility (激励相容); and investment promotion (招商引资) — the core local-government function of attracting industry.
第二章　财税与政府行为 (Fiscal taxation and government behavior). The fiscal underpinnings of the developmental state: the tax-sharing reform of 1994 (分税制改革); land finance (土地财政) — local governments’ reliance on land sales and the revenue it generates; and vertical and horizontal imbalance (纵向不平衡与横向不平衡) between central and local, and among regions.
第三章　政府投融资与债务 (Government investment, financing, and debt). The machinery of local investment: Urban Investment / local financing platforms (城投公司) and land finance as land-financialization (土地金融); local government debt (地方政府债务); and the incentives of local officials in investment promotion (招商引资中的地方官员) — career incentives and the “promotion tournament.”
第四章　工业化中的政府角色 (The government’s role in industrialization). Case studies of state-guided industry: BOE and government investment (京东方与政府投资); the photovoltaic industry and government subsidies (光伏发展与政府补贴); and government industrial guidance funds (政府产业引导基金).
Part 2 — Macro phenomena (下篇 宏观现象)
第五章　城市化与不平衡 (Urbanization and imbalance). Housing prices and household debt (房价与居民债务); imbalance and factor-market reform (不平衡与要素市场改革); and economic development and inequality (经济发展与贫富差距).
第六章　债务与风险 (Debt and risk). Debt and economic recession (债务与经济衰退); why debt piles up — the lessons of Europe and America (债台为何高筑：欧美的教训); China’s debt and risk (中国的债务与风险); and resolving debt risk (化解债务风险).
第七章　国内国际失衡 (Domestic-international imbalance). Low consumption and overcapacity (低消费与产能过剩); the Sino-US trade conflict (中美贸易冲突); and rebalancing and the domestic great cycle (再平衡与国内大循环).
第八章　总结：政府与经济发展 (Conclusion: government and economic development). Competition among regions (地区间竞争); the development and transformation of government (政府的发展与转型); and development goals and process (发展目标与发展过程) — the synthesis of the whole argument.
结束语 — Conclusion
The closing statement on government and the market in China’s development.
Relation to the other sources
This is the first contemporary political-economy analysis on the shelf — distinct from the historical sources, and the natural “what does the PRC look like now” complement:

Where the PRC textbooks give the official history and the Deng biography gives the man, 置身事内 is a primary-source window onto Chinese political economy as of 2021 — land finance, local-government debt, the urban-investment platforms, industrial policy, and the Sino-US trade conflict — written from inside the Chinese economics profession for a broad readership.

sources/zhongguo-gongchandang-lishi-v1-x.content:
History of the Chinese Communist Party, Volume I, Lower Book (Zhongguo Gongchandang lishi 中国共产党历史 第一卷 下册), 1921–1949 — Central Party History Research Office 中共中央党史研究室
What this is
《中国共产党历史》第一卷（1921—1949）下册 is the lower half of the official two-book first volume of the History of the Chinese Communist Party, compiled by the Central Party History Research Office of the CCP (中共中央党史研究室) and issued by the CCP History Press (中共党史出版社; this file is the 2011 printing associated with DuXiu ssid 13029078). Volume I as a whole covers the party from its founding through the founding of the PRC; this lower book alone carries the narrative from the full outbreak of the War of Resistance against Japan in July 1937 through the close of the nationwide Liberation War and the eve of the new state in September 1949.
It is not a private scholarly monograph. It is the central party-history office’s authorized continuous narrative for the late revolutionary period: war, base-area construction, united-front politics, land reform, decisive campaigns, and the transfer from war to state-founding. The voice is institutional and teleological — two destinies, two futures; resistance, solidarity, and progress as the wartime line; the new-democratic revolution’s victory as the book’s terminal meaning. Readers who want the same years from other angles will still need Mao’s Selected Works, Chiang’s diary extracts, and the PRC textbooks already on this shelf; this volume is the party-office synthesis of the 1937–49 arc.
Printed pagination in this edition runs pp. 461–845 for the lower book (the upper book of Vol. I ends before that block). The physical PDF in the wiki root is a full DuXiu-style scan of the lower book only (398 PDF pages including front matter, TOC, body, afterword, and map plates).

How it is organized
Two large 编 (parts) after the shared Vol. I front matter, then a formal 结束语 (conclusion) and 后记 (afterword).

Chapter grain is standard official-history: each 章 opens with a period thesis, then numbered 节 (sections) and titled subheads (strategy, base areas, united front, land, campaigns, congresses).
Chapter breakdown (lower book)
Style: English title + (pinyin + 中文) + multi-line gloss of what the chapter actually holds. Section titles follow the book’s own TOC (OCR-corrected where clear).
第四编 — The party in the nationwide War of Resistance (党在全民族抗日战争时期, July 1937 – August 1945)
第十四章 — Realization of the nationwide War of Resistance; the party’s military-strategic course (实现全面抗战和党的军事战略方针)
Printed open p. 461. Frames the jump from partial to full national resistance after July 1937: the strategic choice facing the party, the building of the anti-Japanese national united front with the Guomindang, and the military line for regular and guerrilla war. Early sections walk the outbreak of comprehensive resistance and the establishment of the anti-Japanese national united front; the middle of the chapter treats the party’s military-strategic guidelines and the creation and expansion of behind-enemy-lines base areas; later sections cover united-front work in the Guomindang-held zones, mass mobilization, and the ideological–political work that the office presents as binding the war effort to party leadership of the people’s war.
第十五章 — Upholding the line of resistance, unity, and progress (坚持抗战、团结、进步的方针)
Printed open p. 525. Opens on the arrival of the strategic stalemate after the fall of Guangzhou and Wuhan (October 1938): Japanese force dispersal, economic strain, and the enemy’s shift of political emphasis. Develops the triad 抗战·团结·进步 against 投降·分裂·倒退 — the office’s formula for holding the united front while opposing friction and capitulation. Substantive threads include Japanese strategy adjustment, the long stalemate battlefield, political struggle inside the united front, and the party’s insistence on independent guerrilla warfare and base-area consolidation rather than merger into a single Nationalist command.
第十六章 — Consolidating the anti-Japanese democratic positions (巩固抗日民主阵地)
Printed open ~p. 578 (TOC). Recasts the war after 1941: the German–Soviet war and the Pacific War redraw the international map; China formally declares war on Japan, Germany, and Italy; the global anti-fascist war reaches full scale. Domestically the chapter is about holding and hardening the anti-Japanese democratic base areas under tighter Japanese pressure and Nationalist friction — military defense, regime building, rent-and-interest reduction and related rural policy, party rectification currents, and the linkage between liberated-area construction and the wider Allied war.
第十七章 — Enlarging the liberated areas and striving for final victory in the people’s war of resistance (扩大解放区，夺取人民抗战的最后胜利)
Printed open p. 625. From 1943–44 global turning points (Stalingrad, collapse of the Axis partnership in Europe, Midway and Guadalcanal in the Pacific, Burma counter-offensive) to local counter-offensives on the liberated-area fronts. Covers the growth of liberated-area military and political strength, coordination with the final phase of the war of resistance, and the office’s account of the party positioning itself for the postwar contest as Japan collapses. Terminal matter of the part leads into August 1945 and the strategic map set for the next 编.
第五编 — The party in the nationwide War of Liberation (党在全国解放战争时期, August 1945 – September 1949)
第十八章 — Striving for peace and democracy at home (争取实现国内和平民主)
Printed open p. 673. Post-surrender China as a contest of two destinies: the party’s program for an independent, free, democratic, unified, and prosperous new country versus continued Nationalist one-party rule under U.S. support. International and domestic postwar balances; Chongqing negotiations and related political struggle; the Political Consultative Conference (parties and numbers as the book lists them); the twin issues of political democratization and nationalization of the armed forces; and the breakdown path from truce politics toward full-scale civil war. The chapter is the office’s bridge from anti-Japanese united front to liberation-war polarization.
第十九章 — Smash the Nationalist offensive; put the liberated areas on a war footing (以自卫战争粉碎国民党的军事进攻和加强解放区建设)
Defensive–mobile war in the first phase of the civil war: defeating Nationalist offensives, shifting force ratios, and building the liberated areas for sustained war. Land policy and support for the front; organization of rear and militia; coordination of several strategic theaters. The office’s emphasis is dual — military self-defense victories and internal consolidation so the liberated areas can carry a long war.
第二十章 — The second turning point in Chinese revolutionary history (中国革命历史的第二个转折点)
The strategic turn: from defense to strategic attack, the language of a new high tide of Chinese revolution (as in the inner-party directive 迎接中国革命的新高潮), and the joining of liberated-area warfare with Guomindang-area popular movements as two fronts. Includes land-reform high tide and correction of left excesses (reference back to land-struggle documents; Ren Bishi’s speech on land-reform problems; reports from Xi Zhongxun, Deng Xiaoping, and others as the book cites them), party rectification amid rapid membership growth (toward ~2.7 million members by 1947 in the book’s figures), and the operational narrative that sets up the decisive campaigns — including texture such as the Liaoshen fighting (Jinzhou, Tashan blocking, Changchun’s peaceful liberation) sampled in the body OCR.
第二十一章 — Strategic decisive battles and the founding of New China (战略决战的胜利和中华人民共和国的成立)
The terminal military-political arc: strategic decisive engagements, collapse of major Nationalist formations, advance across the country, and preparations to found the new state. Late sections reach the Second Plenum of the Seventh Central Committee at Xibaipo (March 1949) — attendance scale and the shift from rural encirclement to governing cities — and carry the narrative to September 1949 and the threshold of the PRC. Closing military paragraphs in the sampled text note residual campaigns into 1950 as the large-scale liberation war winds down, while the political climax of the chapter remains the founding moment.
结束语 — Basic experience and great significance of the victory of China’s new-democratic revolution (中国新民主主义革命胜利的基本经验和伟大意义)
A formal conclusion, not a narrative chapter. Distills the office’s canonical lessons: party leadership; the united front; armed struggle; and party building as a “great project” under conditions where most members came from peasants and other non-worker strata and the party long lived in rural base areas — thought, organization, and work-style construction; criticism and self-criticism; rectification; resistance to subjectivism, sectarianism, and left/right political errors. Frames the 1937–49 victory as the vindication of new democracy and the premise of the socialist period (taken up in later official volumes, not in this file).
后记 — Afterword (后记)
Short compilation afterword from the Central Party History Research Office on the making of the volume (sources, collective authorship, edition line). Treat as paratext for provenance, not as narrative history.
Maps (附图)
Terminal situation and campaign maps (OCR captions include, among others, Eighth Route / New Fourth Army and South China guerrilla strategic counter-offensive, August–September 1945; national military situation at victory in the war of resistance, September 1945; route of the shift of the Center in northern Shaanxi, March 1947 – March 1948). Useful as the book’s own spatial digest of the lower-book years.
How this sits on the shelf

Upstream in Vol. I (not in this PDF): founding of the party, first civil war / land-revolution period, and the run-up through the Xi’an Incident to mid-1937 live in the upper book of the same first volume.
Parallel primary texture: [[mao-zedong-xuanji-4vols|Mao’s Selected Works]] for theoretical and directive voice; Chiang diary selections for the Nationalist high command’s day-grain; [[deng-xiaoping-lushi-li-xinzhi|Deng shilu]] for one marshal-politician’s biographical cut through Taihang and the Central Plains.
Downstream official arc: He Qin PRC history and 2022 马工程 PRC history pick up from 1949; this lower book stops at the founding threshold.
